lessons.title: Square numbers and geometric arrays
lessons.summary: A square number counts a square array: n equal rows, with n objects in each row. The total is n × n, written n².
objectives: Explain square numbers and geometric arrays.
Calculate and interpret area using n² = n × n.
Recognize why this claim fails: n² means 2n.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A square number counts a square array: n equal rows, with n objects in each row. The total is n × n, written n².
The exponent 2 records two equal factors. A 5-by-5 arrangement has 25 cells; doubling the side gives four times the area because both the rows and columns double.

sections.heading: Work through the method
paragraphs: Choose a whole-number side n. Count n cells in one row and multiply by n rows. Check that the total can be arranged with no gaps in a square. When the question gives area instead, reverse this reasoning to find the side.

sections.heading: Connect and check
paragraphs: For n=5, n²=25 while 2n=10. The two expressions count different things.
Remember: Square means equal rows and columns, not multiply by two.

lessons.title: Perfect-square digit and factor patterns
lessons.summary: A positive integer is a perfect square exactly when every exponent in its prime factorisation is even.
objectives: Explain perfect-square digit and factor patterns.
Calculate and interpret positive divisor count, perfect square? using d(n) = ∏(eᵢ + 1).
Recognize why this claim fails: Every number ending in 1 is square.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A positive integer is a perfect square exactly when every exponent in its prime factorisation is even.

Each prime factor of a square comes from multiplying two identical factorisations. Positive divisors pair as d and n/d; only the square root pairs with itself. Therefore perfect squares have an odd number of positive divisors.

sections.heading: Work through the method
paragraphs: Write n as a product of prime powers. Check each exponent for evenness. A last digit of 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 is possible for a square, but is only a quick screening test: 26 ends in 6 and is not square.

sections.heading: Connect and check
paragraphs: Ending in 1 is necessary for some squares, not sufficient. For example, 21 is not a square.
Remember: Even prime exponents make a square; an allowed last digit only makes a candidate.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: A repeated prime factor is one multiplication unit. Pair factors for a square root, group triples for a cube root, and compare prime powers when finding an HCF or LCM.
For the initial values, Perfect square? = Yes; Last digit = 4; Positive divisor count = 15. d(n) = ∏(eᵢ + 1)

lessons.title: Consecutive squares and sums of odd numbers
lessons.summary: The difference between consecutive squares is an odd number: (n+1)²−n²=2n+1.
objectives: Explain consecutive squares and sums of odd numbers.
Calculate and interpret odd border, new area using (n+1)² − n² = 2n + 1.
Recognize why this claim fails: Any set of n odd numbers sums to n².

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: The difference between consecutive squares is an odd number: (n+1)²−n²=2n+1.
Grow an n-by-n square by adding an n-cell strip on two sides and one corner cell. The new border contains n+n+1 cells. Repeating these odd borders explains why the first n odd numbers sum to n².

sections.heading: Work through the method
paragraphs: Expand (n+1)² or draw the added border. Subtract the old area n². For a sum 1+3+...+(2n−1), count n odd terms rather than confusing the last term with the number of terms.

sections.heading: Connect and check
paragraphs: The starting point and spacing matter. For instance, 3+5+7=15, not 3².
Remember: Next square = old square + next odd number.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: (n+1)² − n² = 2n + 1. Start with 5² = 25. Add 5 cells on two edges and one corner: 11. The new area is 36.
For the initial values, Old area = 25; Odd border = 11; New area = 36. (n+1)² − n² = 2n + 1

lessons.title: Squares and triangular numbers
lessons.summary: Triangular numbers count rows of 1, 2, 3, ..., n dots. Two consecutive triangular numbers combine to form a square.
objectives: Explain squares and triangular numbers.
Calculate and interpret first triangular number, combined square using Tₙ + Tₙ₊₁ = (n+1)².
Recognize why this claim fails: Tₙ equals n².

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Triangular numbers count rows of 1, 2, 3, ..., n dots. Two consecutive triangular numbers combine to form a square.
Tₙ=n(n+1)/2 because two identical triangular arrays form an n-by-(n+1) rectangle. Adding Tₙ and Tₙ₊₁ instead gives (n+1)²; the two arrays have different heights.

sections.heading: Work through the method
paragraphs: Compute each triangular number before adding. Keep the subscript tied to the number of rows. Alternatively factor the shared (n+1): n(n+1)/2+(n+1)(n+2)/2=(n+1)².

sections.heading: Connect and check
paragraphs: A triangular arrangement has unequal row lengths; a square has n equal rows. T₄=10 but 4²=16.
Remember: Equal triangles make a rectangle; consecutive triangles make a square.

sections.heading: Read the visualization

lessons.title: Square roots by prime factorisation
lessons.summary: Prime factorisation finds a square root by pairing identical prime factors. One factor from each pair leaves the root.
objectives: Explain square roots by prime factorisation.
Calculate and interpret outside factor, remaining radicand, numerical root using ⁽2⁾√n = outside × ⁽2⁾√inside.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Prime factorisation finds a square root by pairing identical prime factors. One factor from each pair leaves the root.
If n contains p², its root contains p. More generally √(p²ᵃ)=pᵃ for positive primes. An unpaired factor means the square root is not an integer, although a simplified radical can still be written.

sections.heading: Work through the method
paragraphs: Factor the radicand fully. Group identical primes in pairs. Multiply one prime from each complete pair outside the root and leave any unpaired factors inside. Verify by squaring the simplified expression.

sections.heading: Connect and check
paragraphs: Square roots do not distribute over addition: √(9+16)=5, while √9+√16=7.
Remember: Pair inside, one outside.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: A repeated prime factor is one multiplication unit. Pair factors for a square root, group triples for a cube root, and compare prime powers when finding an HCF or LCM.

lessons.title: Estimating square roots between integers
lessons.summary: A nonnegative number can be located between consecutive perfect squares to bound its square root.
objectives: Explain estimating square roots between integers.
Calculate and interpret lower bound, upper bound, approximate root using k² ≤ n ≤ (k+1)².
Recognize why this claim fails: √50 is exactly 7.1.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A nonnegative number can be located between consecutive perfect squares to bound its square root.
Squaring preserves order for nonnegative values. Thus 7²<60<8² implies 7<√60<8. A decimal approximation is useful but remains different from an exact value or a proven interval.

sections.heading: Work through the method
paragraphs: List nearby squares and find the bounding pair. Refine with tenths if needed by squaring the trial values. Label every rounded answer as approximate and check its square against the original number.

sections.heading: Connect and check
paragraphs: 7.1²=50.41, so 7.1 is an upper bound here, not the exact root.
Remember: Bracket with squares before reaching for decimals.

sections.heading: Read the visualization

For the initial values, Lower bound = 7; Upper bound = 8; Approximate root = 7.74596669. k² ≤ n ≤ (k+1)²

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: The number 1729 can be written as a sum of two positive integer cubes in two different ways: 1³+12³ and 9³+10³.

lessons.title: Repeated doubling and exponential growth
lessons.summary: Repeated doubling is multiplicative growth: each stage multiplies the current amount by 2. After n stages, the amount is Q₀2ⁿ.
objectives: Explain repeated doubling and exponential growth.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Repeated doubling is multiplicative growth: each stage multiplies the current amount by 2. After n stages, the amount is Q₀2ⁿ.

The stage counter begins at zero with the starting amount. Adding 2 each stage makes linear growth, a different process. In a paper-folding model, the thickness formula is idealised: real paper cannot be folded arbitrarily many times.

sections.heading: Work through the method

sections.heading: Connect and check
paragraphs: That expression adds a fixed amount. Doubling uses the current total as the next multiplicand.
Remember: Count multiplications, not additions.

objectives: Explain multiplying and dividing powers with a common base.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: For powers with the same nonzero base, multiplication adds exponents and division subtracts them.
b³ contains three copies of b. Multiplying by b⁴ contributes four more copies, giving seven altogether. Division cancels repeated copies, which also explains why a negative exponent is a reciprocal.

sections.heading: Work through the method

sections.heading: Connect and check

Remember: Same base: multiply → add; divide → subtract.

lessons.summary: A power of a power multiplies exponents: (bᵃ)ᶜ=bᵃᶜ. Powers of a product distribute to each factor.
objectives: Explain power of a power and powers of products.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A power of a power multiplies exponents: (bᵃ)ᶜ=bᵃᶜ. Powers of a product distribute to each factor.

The outer exponent repeats the entire inner block. For example, (2³)² contains two blocks of three copies of 2, giving six copies. A product is different from a sum: (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ but (a+b)ⁿ does not generally split.

sections.heading: Work through the method
paragraphs: Identify the parentheses and the operation inside them. Multiply exponents for a powered power. Raise every factor in a product to the outer power. Check the expanded repeated multiplication for a small example.

sections.heading: Connect and check

Remember: Power of power: multiply counts. Product power: power every factor.

lessons.title: Zero exponents and nonzero-base restrictions
lessons.summary: Any nonzero number raised to the zero power equals 1. This keeps the exponent laws consistent.
objectives: Explain zero exponents and nonzero-base restrictions.
Calculate and interpret zero power using b⁰ = bᵃ/bᵃ = 1, b ≠ 0.
Recognize why this claim fails: The zero exponent makes the value zero.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Any nonzero number raised to the zero power equals 1. This keeps the exponent laws consistent.
For b≠0, b³/b³=1. The quotient rule also gives b^(3−3)=b⁰. The two calculations must agree. This argument cannot use b=0 because 0/0 is undefined.

sections.heading: Work through the method
paragraphs: Start with equal nonzero powers in numerator and denominator. Cancel their values to obtain 1, then subtract the equal exponents to obtain 0. State the nonzero restriction explicitly rather than extending the argument to 0⁰.

sections.heading: Connect and check
paragraphs: The exponent is a factor-count rule, not multiplication by zero.
Remember: Zero copies in an exponent rule give the multiplicative identity 1.

sections.heading: Read the visualization

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Scientific notation writes a nonzero number as c×10ᵉ with 1≤|c|<10 and integer e. This separates the leading digits from the scale.

The coefficient supplies significant information; the exponent supplies magnitude. For 45000 the normalized form is 4.5×10⁴. Although 45×10³ has the same value, it is not normalized scientific notation.

sections.heading: Work through the method
paragraphs: Move the decimal until the absolute coefficient is at least 1 and less than 10. Count the place-value shifts to find the exponent. Large magnitudes usually need positive exponents; magnitudes below 1 need negative exponents. Reconstruct the number to check the sign.

objectives: Explain comparing quantities in scientific notation.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: To compare positive numbers in normalized scientific notation, compare exponents first and coefficients second.

Coefficients between 1 and 10 cannot outweigh a whole exponent step: 9.9×10⁴ is smaller than 1.1×10⁵. If exponents match, ordinary coefficient order decides. Negative values require attention to sign before magnitude.

lessons.title: Power Play: guided examples and applications
lessons.summary: Apply repeated doubling and exponential growth; multiplying and dividing powers with a common base; power of a power and powers of products through explained numerical problems.
objectives: Explain power play: guided examples and applications.
Calculate and interpret initial, stages, final using Qₖ = Q₀ × 2ᵏ.
Recognize why this claim fails: n doublings give Q₀+2n.

sections.heading: Retrieval before calculation
paragraphs: Qₙ=Q₀2ⁿ. The stage counter begins at zero with the starting amount. Adding 2 each stage makes linear growth, a different process. In a paper-folding model, the thickness formula is idealised: real paper cannot be folded arbitrarily many times. Conditions: The model assumes exact doubling at each stage; real physical constraints are separate.

bᵃbᶜ=bᵃ⁺ᶜ; bᵃ/bᶜ=bᵃ⁻ᶜ. b³ contains three copies of b. Multiplying by b⁴ contributes four more copies, giving seven altogether. Division cancels repeated copies, which also explains why a negative exponent is a reciprocal. Conditions: The quotient rule requires b≠0. The common-base condition is essential.

(bᵃ)ᶜ=bᵃᶜ; (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ. The outer exponent repeats the entire inner block. For example, (2³)² contains two blocks of three copies of 2, giving six copies. A product is different from a sum: (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ but (a+b)ⁿ does not generally split. Conditions: Rules shown use integer powers; negative powers require nonzero factors.

sections.heading: Repeated doubling and exponential growth
paragraphs: Repeated doubling is multiplicative growth: each stage multiplies the current amount by 2. After n stages, the amount is Q₀2ⁿ.
Record the initial amount. Multiply by 2 once for each stage, or use 2ⁿ to combine the repeated factors. Check n=0 before interpreting the table so the first doubling is not counted twice.
Remember: Count multiplications, not additions.

sections.heading: Multiplying and dividing powers with a common base
paragraphs: For powers with the same nonzero base, multiplication adds exponents and division subtracts them.
Confirm the bases are equal before combining exponents. Use addition for multiplication and subtraction for division. Keep the order of the numerator and denominator; b²/b⁵=b⁻³, not b³.
Remember: Same base: multiply → add; divide → subtract.

sections.heading: Power of a power and powers of products
paragraphs: A power of a power multiplies exponents: (bᵃ)ᶜ=bᵃᶜ. Powers of a product distribute to each factor.

Identify the parentheses and the operation inside them. Multiply exponents for a powered power. Raise every factor in a product to the outer power. Check the expanded repeated multiplication for a small example.
Remember: Power of power: multiply counts. Product power: power every factor.

sections.heading: Review your errors
paragraphs: n doublings give Q₀+2n. Correction: That expression adds a fixed amount. Doubling uses the current total as the next multiplicand.
Add exponents when adding powers. Correction: 2²+2³=4+8=12, not 2⁵. The exponent rule applies to multiplication.
(a+b)²=a²+b². Correction: The cross term is missing. (a+b)²=a²+2ab+b².

paragraphs: Qₖ = Q₀ × 2ᵏ. Initial amount: 1. Each stage multiplies the amount by 2. After 6 stages: 1 × 2^6 = 64.

sections.heading: Need for numeral systems and counting symbols
paragraphs: Compare a tally count with positional notation. Writing 999 as repeated unit marks needs 999 marks, whereas three decimal digits suffice. objectives: Explain roman numerals and additive/subtractive rules.

sections.heading: Roman numerals and additive/subtractive rules
paragraphs: Roman notation uses landmark symbols I, V, X, L, C, D and M. A numeral combines additive groups and conventional subtractive groups such as IV or IX. Work from the largest permitted group downward. After choosing a group, subtract its value and continue. Decode the completed numeral to check the total. Use only the conventional subtractive pairs; arbitrary smaller-before-larger combinations are not valid.

sections.heading: Why the method works

lessons.title: Place value and the base of a number system
lessons.summary: A positional system gives a digit its value from both its symbol and its position. In base b the places are 1, b, b², b³ and so on.
objectives: Explain place value and the base of a number system.
Calculate and interpret representation, base, decimal value using N = Σ digit × base^position.
Recognize why this claim fails: Every numeral system uses exactly the same place weights.

sections.heading: Place value and the base of a number system
paragraphs: A positional system gives a digit its value from both its symbol and its position. In base b the places are 1, b, b², b³ and so on. To decode, multiply each digit by its place weight and add. To encode a nonnegative integer, repeatedly divide by the base and read the remainders backwards. Check by converting the representation back to the original number.
A positional system gives a digit its value from both its symbol and its position. In base b the places are 1, b, b², b³ and so on.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Only digits 0 through b−1 are allowed. A zero digit holds an empty place: 101 in base 2 means one four, zero twos and one unit. Without its position, a digit alone cannot tell the full contribution.

To decode, multiply each digit by its place weight and add. To encode a nonnegative integer, repeatedly divide by the base and read the remainders backwards. Check by converting the representation back to the original number.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: Egyptian additive notation and calendar-style Mayan weights illustrate why the convention must be stated.
Recall cue: Position supplies a power; the digit counts that power.

paragraphs: Each place or landmark contributes its value times its count. Positional systems assign weights by position; additive systems use landmark symbols. Identify the convention before adding contributions.

lessons.title: Definition and classification of quadrilaterals
lessons.summary: Quadrilaterals are closed figures with four straight sides. Particular side, angle and diagonal conditions identify special classes.
objectives: Explain definition and classification of quadrilaterals.
Calculate and interpret classification using d₁²=a²+b²+2ab cos θ; d₂²=a²+b²−2ab cos θ.
Recognize why this claim fails: A rhombus must have right angles.

sections.heading: Definition and classification of quadrilaterals
paragraphs: Use inclusive definitions: every square belongs to the rectangles and to the rhombi, and both are parallelograms. A property is necessary when every member has it; it is sufficient when it forces membership. Equal diagonals are necessary for rectangles but insufficient among arbitrary quadrilaterals. Classify by stated properties rather than visual orientation.
Quadrilaterals are closed figures with four straight sides. Particular side, angle and diagonal conditions identify special classes.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles; a rhombus is a parallelogram with equal sides. A square satisfies both. Properties must not be confused with a picture that only looks like a special case: a diagram can suggest a claim, while congruence and angle reasoning prove it.

State the given properties, identify which class they force, and justify each conclusion. In the tool a parallelogram is built from two sides and an included angle. Try equal sides, a right angle, or both; then compare the diagonals and area.

sections.heading: Constructing rectangles from diagonal conditions
paragraphs: Construct two equal segments through a common midpoint and join their endpoints cyclically. Their bisection makes a parallelogram; their equality then forces a rectangle. The crossing angle changes the aspect ratio. Equal diagonals alone, without bisection, are insufficient: an isosceles trapezium supplies a counterexample.
Equal diagonal segments that bisect each other determine a rectangle when their endpoints are joined in cyclic order.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Bisection makes the quadrilateral a parallelogram. In a parallelogram, equal diagonals force adjacent side triangles into an equality that yields right angles. Equality without bisection is insufficient: an isosceles trapezium can also have equal diagonals.

Locate a common midpoint and draw both equal diagonals through it. Join successive endpoints, not opposite endpoints. Use triangle congruence or the diagonal-square identity to justify the right angles. Vary the crossing angle to see many rectangles, including the square case.

sections.heading: Quadrilateral constructions and investigations
paragraphs: Construct two equal segments through a common midpoint and join their endpoints cyclically. Their bisection makes a parallelogram; their equality then forces a rectangle. The crossing angle changes the aspect ratio. Equal diagonals alone, without bisection, are insufficient: an isosceles trapezium supplies a counterexample.
Equal diagonal segments that bisect each other determine a rectangle when their endpoints are joined in cyclic order.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Bisection makes the quadrilateral a parallelogram. In a parallelogram, equal diagonals force adjacent side triangles into an equality that yields right angles. Equality without bisection is insufficient: an isosceles trapezium can also have equal diagonals.

Locate a common midpoint and draw both equal diagonals through it. Join successive endpoints, not opposite endpoints. Use triangle congruence or the diagonal-square identity to justify the right angles. Vary the crossing angle to see many rectangles, including the square case.

lessons.title: Kite properties and diagonals
lessons.summary: A kite can be constructed with two pairs of adjacent equal sides. In the symmetric construction its diagonals are perpendicular, and one diagonal bisects the other.
objectives: Explain kite properties and diagonals.
Calculate and interpret vertical diagonal, horizontal diagonal, area using Area = diagonal₁ × diagonal₂ / 2.
Recognize why this claim fails: Every kite has two diagonals that bisect each other.

sections.heading: Kite properties and diagonals
paragraphs: A kite can be constructed with two pairs of adjacent equal sides. In the symmetric construction its diagonals are perpendicular, and one diagonal bisects the other. Mark the symmetry axis and equal adjacent sides. Distinguish the full diagonals from their halves. Add the two vertical halves, double the horizontal half, then apply the perpendicular-diagonal area formula. Explain which bisection claim is supported.
A kite can be constructed with two pairs of adjacent equal sides. In the symmetric construction its diagonals are perpendicular, and one diagonal bisects the other.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Do not transfer every rhombus property to a kite. Unless the top and bottom halves agree, the horizontal diagonal does not bisect the vertical one. With perpendicular diagonals, four right triangles give area equal to half the product of the diagonal lengths.

Mark the symmetry axis and equal adjacent sides. Distinguish the full diagonals from their halves. Add the two vertical halves, double the horizontal half, then apply the perpendicular-diagonal area formula. Explain which bisection claim is supported.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: In this model the vertical halves can be unequal even though the horizontal halves are equal.
Recall cue: A kite can have one bisecting diagonal without both bisecting.

lessons.title: Reasoning from sufficient and necessary properties

objectives: Explain reasoning from sufficient and necessary properties.

sections.heading: Reasoning from sufficient and necessary properties
paragraphs: Use inclusive definitions: every square belongs to the rectangles and to the rhombi, and both are parallelograms. A property is necessary when every member has it; it is sufficient when it forces membership. Equal diagonals are necessary for rectangles but insufficient among arbitrary quadrilaterals. Classify by stated properties rather than visual orientation.
Quadrilaterals are closed figures with four straight sides. Particular side, angle and diagonal conditions identify special classes.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles; a rhombus is a parallelogram with equal sides. A square satisfies both. Properties must not be confused with a picture that only looks like a special case: a diagram can suggest a claim, while congruence and angle reasoning prove it.

sections.heading: Definition and classification of quadrilaterals
paragraphs: Use inclusive definitions: every square belongs to the rectangles and to the rhombi, and both are parallelograms. A property is necessary when every member has it; it is sufficient when it forces membership. Equal diagonals are necessary for rectangles but insufficient among arbitrary quadrilaterals. Classify by stated properties rather than visual orientation.

A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles; a rhombus is a parallelogram with equal sides. A square satisfies both. Properties must not be confused with a picture that only looks like a special case: a diagram can suggest a claim, while congruence and angle reasoning prove it. State the given properties, identify which class they force, and justify each conclusion. In the tool a parallelogram is built from two sides and an included angle. Try equal sides, a right angle, or both; then compare the diagonals and area.
Remember: Equal sides gives rhombus; right angle gives rectangle; both gives square.

sections.heading: Diagonals bisect each other: rectangle proof
paragraphs: Let rectangle diagonals AC and BD intersect at O. Opposite sides are equal and parallel, so alternate interior angles and ASA give triangles AOB and COD congruent. Corresponding parts give AO=CO and BO=DO. Equal diagonal lengths are a separate property: bisection holds for every parallelogram.

sections.heading: Multiples and general algebraic number forms
paragraphs: Division with remainder writes a nonnegative integer as n=dq+r, where d is positive and 0≤r<d. Divide to count complete groups. sections.heading: Why the method works

sections.heading: Remainders and numbers of the form kn+r
paragraphs: Division with remainder writes a nonnegative integer as n=dq+r, where d is positive and 0≤r<d. Divide to count complete groups. Multiply the quotient by the divisor, then subtract from the dividend. Check the reconstruction and the remainder bounds. A general number with a specified remainder can be written dq+r with variable whole-number q.
Division with remainder writes a nonnegative integer as n=dq+r, where d is positive and 0≤r<d.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The quotient counts complete groups and the remainder counts leftovers. The remainder restriction makes the representation unique: without it, shifting one group between q and r would create many descriptions. Multiples of d are exactly the cases with remainder zero.

lessons.title: Divisibility by 2, 5 and 10
lessons.summary: A divisibility test predicts a zero remainder using place value instead of long division. The correct test depends on the divisor.
objectives: Explain divisibility by 2, 5 and 10.
Calculate and interpret last two digits, last three digits using 10≡1 (mod 3,9); 10≡−1 (mod 11).
Recognize why this claim fails: A digit-sum rule works for every divisor.

sections.heading: Divisibility by 2, 5 and 10
paragraphs: Write a number as a sum of decimal place contributions. Since 10 is divisible by 2,5,10, only the last digit matters for these divisors. Since 100 is divisible by 4 and 1000 by 8, use the last two or three digits. Since 10≡1 modulo 3 and 9, use digit sums; since 10≡−1 modulo 11, use alternating sums. A zero sum is divisible by each applicable divisor.
A divisibility test predicts a zero remainder using place value instead of long division. The correct test depends on the divisor.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: For 3 and 9, every power of ten leaves remainder 1, so the digit sum has the same remainder as the full number. For 11, powers of ten alternate between remainders 1 and −1. For 4 and 8, the last two or three digits suffice because earlier place values are divisible by the divisor.

Choose the divisor first, apply its matching digit or suffix test, and verify with a remainder. Being divisible by 2 does not guarantee divisibility by 4. A rule is established from place-value algebra, while a single numerical check illustrates it.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: For 4 and 8 use suffixes; for 11 use alternating sums. The tests have different place-value reasons.
Recall cue: Match the test to the divisor; place value explains why.

sections.heading: Read the visualization

lessons.title: Cryptarithms with addition and carrying
lessons.summary: A cryptarithm replaces digits with letters while preserving arithmetic. Repeated letters mean the same digit; different letters normally mean different digits.
objectives: Explain cryptarithms with addition and carrying.
Calculate and interpret result, b, c, valid distinct-letter assignment? using A+A=BC or A×A=BC.
Recognize why this claim fails: Arithmetic equality alone makes a valid letter assignment.

sections.heading: Cryptarithms with addition and carrying
paragraphs: A repeated letter must have one fixed digit, different letters must have different digits, and a leading digit cannot be zero. In A+A=BC, carrying requires 2A≥10. A=7 gives 7+7=14 with all three digits distinct. In A×A=BC, A=8 gives 64. Systematically reject assignments that violate carrying, distinctness or leading-zero rules.
A cryptarithm replaces digits with letters while preserving arithmetic. Repeated letters mean the same digit; different letters normally mean different digits.

sections.heading: Cryptarithms with multiplication and constraints
paragraphs: A repeated letter must have one fixed digit, different letters must have different digits, and a leading digit cannot be zero. In A+A=BC, carrying requires 2A≥10. A=7 gives 7+7=14 with all three digits distinct. In A×A=BC, A=8 gives 64. Systematically reject assignments that violate carrying, distinctness or leading-zero rules.

sections.heading: Divisibility by 2, 5 and 10
paragraphs: Write a number as a sum of decimal place contributions. Since 10 is divisible by 2,5,10, only the last digit matters for these divisors. Since 100 is divisible by 4 and 1000 by 8, use the last two or three digits. Since 10≡1 modulo 3 and 9, use digit sums; since 10≡−1 modulo 11, use alternating sums. A zero sum is divisible by each applicable divisor.

For 3 and 9, every power of ten leaves remainder 1, so the digit sum has the same remainder as the full number. For 11, powers of ten alternate between remainders 1 and −1. For 4 and 8, the last two or three digits suffice because earlier place values are divisible by the divisor. Choose the divisor first, apply its matching digit or suffix test, and verify with a remainder. Being divisible by 2 does not guarantee divisibility by 4. A rule is established from place-value algebra, while a single numerical check illustrates it.

sections.heading: Distributive law using area and arithmetic
paragraphs: The distributive law multiplies every term inside a bracket by the outside factor: a(b+c)=ab+ac. Calculate the bracket total and multiply once. Separately calculate each partial product and add. Their equality checks the expansion. For a subtraction rewrite the second term with its sign before multiplying.
The distributive law multiplies every term inside a bracket by the outside factor: a(b+c)=ab+ac.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: An area split into two adjoining rectangles gives the same total as the unsplit rectangle when lengths are nonnegative. The algebraic identity also works for signed numbers. Using it for subtraction means distributing the minus sign or negative factor to every term.

sections.heading: Changes in products when factors increase
paragraphs: If factors increase from a,b to a+h,b+k, the product changes by ak+bh+hk. The hk corner is easily missed. For 10×20 changing to 11×22, the increase is 10×2+20×1+1×2=42, hence the new product is 242. Equal percentage growth in both factors compounds rather than simply adding.

lessons.title: Square of a sum: geometric derivation
lessons.summary: An algebraic identity is true for every permitted input. Squaring a sum produces a², two cross products ab, and b².
objectives: Explain square of a sum: geometric derivation.
Calculate and interpret square of sum, cross term using (a+b)²=a²+2ab+b².
Recognize why this claim fails: The square of a sum is the sum of squares.

sections.heading: Square of a sum: geometric derivation
paragraphs: An (a+b)-square splits into a², two ab rectangles and b², proving (a+b)²=a²+2ab+b². Substituting −b gives (a−b)²=a²−2ab+b². Multiplying (a+b)(a−b) cancels cross terms and gives a²−b². Check a proposed identity by expansion; one counterexample can reject an incorrect identity but a few matches do not prove it.
An algebraic identity is true for every permitted input. Squaring a sum produces a², two cross products ab, and b².

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The four products in (a+b)(a+b) are a², ab, ba and b². Combining the two equal cross products gives 2ab. Replacing b with −b explains the square-of-difference identity. Multiplying a sum and difference cancels the cross terms instead.
Expand one factor against every term in the other. Collect like terms and keep their signs. Test a numerical example to catch a mistake, then use the symbolic expansion for the general explanation.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: The two cross products are missing. Compare (7+3)²=100 with 7²+3²=58.

lessons.title: Equivalent algebraic descriptions of a pattern
lessons.summary: The distributive law multiplies every term inside a bracket by the outside factor: a(b+c)=ab+ac.
objectives: Explain equivalent algebraic descriptions of a pattern.
Calculate and interpret distributed value, first partial product, second partial product using a(b+c)=ab+ac.
Recognize why this claim fails: Multiply only the first term inside a bracket.

sections.heading: Equivalent algebraic descriptions of a pattern
paragraphs: The distributive law multiplies every term inside a bracket by the outside factor: a(b+c)=ab+ac. Calculate the bracket total and multiply once. Separately calculate each partial product and add. Their equality checks the expansion. For a subtraction rewrite the second term with its sign before multiplying.
The distributive law multiplies every term inside a bracket by the outside factor: a(b+c)=ab+ac.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: An area split into two adjoining rectangles gives the same total as the unsplit rectangle when lengths are nonnegative. The algebraic identity also works for signed numbers. Using it for subtraction means distributing the minus sign or negative factor to every term.

Calculate the bracket total and multiply once. Separately calculate each partial product and add. Their equality checks the expansion. For a subtraction rewrite the second term with its sign before multiplying.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: Both terms must receive the outside factor. With a negative factor, both signs need attention.
Recall cue: One outside factor visits every inside term.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: a(b+c)=ab+ac. Inside the brackets: 8+2=10. Direct calculation: 7×10=70. Distributed calculation: 56+14=70.
For the initial values, Direct value = 70; First partial product = 56; Second partial product = 14; Distributed value = 70. a(b+c)=ab+ac

Direct calculation: 7×10=70.
Distributed calculation: 56+14=70.

sections.heading: Explain your result
paragraphs: outside factor = 16; first bracket term = -10; second bracket term = -5. Find distributed value.
Inside the brackets: -10+-5=-15.
Direct calculation: 16×-15=-240.
Distributed calculation: -160+-80=-240.
Distributed value = -240.
Therefore: -240
One outside factor visits every inside term.
Multiply only the first term inside a bracket.: Both terms must receive the outside factor. With a negative factor, both signs need attention.

lessons.title: Interpreting non-proportional situations
lessons.summary: A relationship y=mx+k has a constant rate m and an initial value k. A nonzero initial value prevents direct proportion.
objectives: Explain interpreting non-proportional situations.
Calculate and interpret total, cost per item using cost=rate×quantity+fixed charge.
Recognize why this claim fails: Any constant-increase relationship is proportional.

sections.heading: Interpreting non-proportional situations
paragraphs: For direct proportion y=kx, y/x is constant and the graph passes through the origin. For inverse proportion y=k/x, xy is constant. A taxi fare y=20+5x has a fixed charge, so it is neither of these relationships. Decide from the invariant and the context rather than from the direction of change alone.
A relationship y=mx+k has a constant rate m and an initial value k. A nonzero initial value prevents direct proportion.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: For a taxi fare with a fixed charge, doubling distance does not double the whole fare. Direct proportion is the special case k=0, where the graph goes through the origin and y/x stays constant. A straight line alone is not enough.

Separate the fixed charge from the per-unit charge. Multiply the unit rate by the quantity, then add the fixed term once. Compare output/input at several positive inputs to test whether it stays constant.

sections.heading: Converting measurement units before forming ratios
paragraphs: Convert units before cancelling: 2 metres : 50 centimetres becomes 200:50=4:1. Writing 2:50 ignores the different units. A dimensionless ratio compares like quantities; a rate can compare different units, such as kilometres per hour, and must retain those units.
A ratio compares quantities multiplicatively and preserves their order. Dividing both terms by the same positive factor produces an equivalent ratio.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: A ratio 3:2 means three equal parts of the first quantity for two parts of the second. It does not mean their difference is always one. Units must be compatible before cancellation, and the denominator term must be nonzero when the ratio is viewed as a quotient.

lessons.title: Density of rational and irrational numbers
lessons.summary: Between two distinct rational numbers there is another rational number, and this construction can be repeated indefinitely. Irrational numbers also occur in every such interval.
objectives: Explain density of rational and irrational numbers.

sections.heading: Density of rational and irrational numbers
paragraphs: Between two distinct rational numbers there is another rational number, and this construction can be repeated indefinitely. Irrational numbers also occur in every such interval. Order the endpoints. Construct their average and verify both inequalities. Repeat on a subinterval to obtain more rationals. For an irrational example use an exact irrational expression, not a finite decimal claimed to be irrational.
Between two distinct rational numbers there is another rational number, and this construction can be repeated indefinitely. Irrational numbers also occur in every such interval.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The average of two rational endpoints is rational and lies strictly inside. For rational a<b, a+(b−a)/√2 is irrational and also inside because 0<1/√2<1. Displayed finite decimals approximate the latter; the formula establishes its irrationality.

lessons.title: Converting recurring decimals to fractions
lessons.summary: A purely recurring decimal repeats a fixed digit block forever. Multiplying by a power of ten aligns the repeated tails so they can be subtracted.
objectives: Explain converting recurring decimals to fractions.
Calculate and interpret reduced numerator, reduced denominator using x=block/(10ᵏ−1).
Recognize why this claim fails: 0.(09) has a one-digit block because the zero has no value.

sections.heading: Converting recurring decimals to fractions
paragraphs: A purely recurring decimal repeats a fixed digit block forever. Multiplying by a power of ten aligns the repeated tails so they can be subtracted. Let x equal the recurring decimal. Count the block length k. Write 10ᵏx, subtract x, solve (10ᵏ−1)x=block and reduce by a common divisor. This tool covers purely recurring decimals; a nonrepeating prefix needs another subtraction setup.
A purely recurring decimal repeats a fixed digit block forever. Multiplying by a power of ten aligns the repeated tails so they can be subtracted.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: For a two-digit block, 100x and x have identical decimal tails. Subtracting leaves 99x equal to the block. The resulting fraction may reduce. A leading zero still counts as a digit in the repeating block.

Let x equal the recurring decimal. Count the block length k. Write 10ᵏx, subtract x, solve (10ᵏ−1)x=block and reduce by a common divisor. This tool covers purely recurring decimals; a nonrepeating prefix needs another subtraction setup.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: Its block has two positions. The denominator is 99, giving 9/99=1/11.

sections.heading: Polynomial versus non-polynomial expressions
paragraphs: A polynomial has finitely many terms with nonnegative integer powers of its variable. Thus 3x²−2x+7 is quadratic, while x⁻¹ and √x are not polynomials in x. Combine like terms before identifying degree: x³−x³+x² has degree 2. A nonzero constant has degree 0; the zero polynomial has no degree under the usual school convention.
A polynomial in x is a finite sum of terms with nonnegative integer powers of x. Coefficients are constants with respect to x.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: A negative power such as x⁻¹ or a fractional power such as x^(1/2) is not a polynomial term. The degree is the largest exponent with nonzero coefficient after simplification. A zero leading coefficient can lower the degree, so inspect the actual expression rather than a label.

Simplify and combine like powers. Check each variable exponent, identify nonzero coefficients, and determine the degree. To evaluate, replace every occurrence of x with the same value and follow the order of operations.

sections.heading: Polynomial versus non-polynomial expressions
paragraphs: A polynomial has finitely many terms with nonnegative integer powers of its variable. Thus 3x²−2x+7 is quadratic, while x⁻¹ and √x are not polynomials in x. Combine like terms before identifying degree: x³−x³+x² has degree 2. A nonzero constant has degree 0; the zero polynomial has no degree under the usual school convention.

A negative power such as x⁻¹ or a fractional power such as x^(1/2) is not a polynomial term. The degree is the largest exponent with nonzero coefficient after simplification. A zero leading coefficient can lower the degree, so inspect the actual expression rather than a label. Simplify and combine like powers. Check each variable exponent, identify nonzero coefficients, and determine the degree. To evaluate, replace every occurrence of x with the same value and follow the order of operations.
Remember: Polynomial powers are whole and nonnegative; zero coefficients do not set degree.

sections.heading: Cartesian axes, origin and coordinate conventions
paragraphs: An ordered pair (x,y) locates a point by horizontal movement first and vertical movement second. The order carries meaning. Start at the origin. Move horizontally by x, then vertically by y. Read the coordinates in that same order. Use a common scale and labelled axes when describing a map; interchanging coordinates usually changes the point.
An ordered pair (x,y) locates a point by horizontal movement first and vertical movement second. The order carries meaning.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The horizontal axis is the x-axis; the vertical axis is the y-axis. Signs identify quadrants away from the axes. A point with x=0 lies on the y-axis, and a point with y=0 lies on the x-axis; neither belongs to a quadrant.

lessons.title: Standard form ax+by+c=0 and its restrictions
lessons.summary: A linear equation in two variables has form ax+by+c=0 with a and b not both zero. A solution is an ordered pair that makes the equation true.
objectives: Explain standard form ax+by+c=0 and its restrictions.
Calculate and interpret residual, solution pair? using ax+by+c=0.
Recognize why this claim fails: One equation in two variables always gives one pair.

sections.heading: Standard form ax+by+c=0 and its restrictions
paragraphs: A genuine linear equation ax+by+c=0 needs a and b not both zero. Checking a pair requires substituting both coordinates and obtaining zero residual. If b≠0, choose any real x and set y=−(ax+c)/b, giving infinitely many real solutions. If b=0 and a≠0, x=−c/a and y is free: this is a vertical line. Contextual integer or nonnegative restrictions may reduce the allowed set.
A linear equation in two variables has form ax+by+c=0 with a and b not both zero. A solution is an ordered pair that makes the equation true.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: One equation ordinarily leaves one degree of freedom, so it has infinitely many real solution pairs. If b≠0, each chosen x determines y. If b=0 and a≠0, x is fixed while y is free. A two-variable equation is different from a pair of equations solved simultaneously.

Substitute both coordinates and calculate the residual ax+by+c. Zero confirms a solution. To generate pairs, choose the free coordinate and solve for the other, checking any nonzero-divisor restriction before division.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: It generally describes an entire line of pairs. A second independent condition is needed for a unique intersection.
Recall cue: A solution pair makes the residual zero.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: A common point satisfies both equations. Parallel distinct lines have no intersection; coincident lines share infinitely many points. Vertical lines need x=constant rather than division by a zero y coefficient.
For the initial values, Residual = 0; Solution pair? = Yes; Required y = 3. ax+by+c=0

sections.heading: Generating multiple solutions of a linear equation
paragraphs: A genuine linear equation ax+by+c=0 needs a and b not both zero. Checking a pair requires substituting both coordinates and obtaining zero residual. If b≠0, choose any real x and set y=−(ax+c)/b, giving infinitely many real solutions. If b=0 and a≠0, x=−c/a and y is free: this is a vertical line. Contextual integer or nonnegative restrictions may reduce the allowed set.

sections.heading: Standard form ax+by+c=0 and its restrictions
paragraphs: A genuine linear equation ax+by+c=0 needs a and b not both zero. Checking a pair requires substituting both coordinates and obtaining zero residual. If b≠0, choose any real x and set y=−(ax+c)/b, giving infinitely many real solutions. If b=0 and a≠0, x=−c/a and y is free: this is a vertical line. Contextual integer or nonnegative restrictions may reduce the allowed set.

To generate pairs, choose the free coordinate and solve for the other, checking any nonzero-divisor restriction before division.

objectives: Explain lines, rays, segments and collinear points.

sections.heading: Lines, rays, segments and collinear points
paragraphs: A segment has two endpoints and finite length. A ray has one endpoint and extends in one direction; a line extends in both directions. Three collinear points lie on the same line. Coordinates can test collinearity using a zero determinant, whereas a drawing supplies an illustration whose thickness and scale limit visual judgement.
An angle measures a turn between rays with a common endpoint. Acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex angles describe different ranges of this turn.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Angles in a linear pair sum to 180°, while angles around a point sum to 360°. These totals come from the straight and full turns. A reflex angle is greater than 180° and less than 360°, not an unusually large acute angle.

Identify the shared vertex and reference rays. Read the degree measure, classify it by its range, and calculate a related angle only when its defining configuration applies. A sum rule alone does not identify a linear pair without the required geometry.

sections.heading: Intersecting and parallel lines

lessons.title: Converse isosceles triangle theorem
lessons.summary: In a triangle, equal sides oppose equal angles. Conversely, equal angles oppose equal sides. These are related but distinct theorem statements.
objectives: Explain converse isosceles triangle theorem.
Calculate and interpret apex angle using apex=180°−2×base angle.
Recognize why this claim fails: The sides beside equal angles must be equal.

sections.heading: Converse isosceles triangle theorem
paragraphs: If base angles B and C of a triangle are equal, their opposite sides AC and AB are equal. A proof draws the angle bisector from A: the two smaller triangles share a side and have equal angles, giving AAS congruence. Equal-side and equal-angle statements are converses and should not be assumed from an unlabelled sketch.
In a triangle, equal sides oppose equal angles. Conversely, equal angles oppose equal sides. These are related but distinct theorem statements.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: To use the converse, the given information must concern equal angles; you then infer equality of their opposite sides. With both base angles θ, the apex angle is 180°−2θ. The angle sum also limits a valid positive base angle to below 90°.

Name the equal angles and identify the sides opposite them. State the converse theorem, then conclude those sides are equal. Calculate the remaining angle from the triangle sum and verify it is positive.

sections.heading: Retrieval before calculation
paragraphs: Area=ab sinθ; perimeter=2(a+b). A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles; a rhombus is a parallelogram with equal sides. A square satisfies both. Properties must not be confused with a picture that only looks like a special case: a diagram can suggest a claim, while congruence and angle reasoning prove it. Conditions: The tool constructs parallelograms only, not arbitrary quadrilaterals. Floating diagonal lengths are approximate; special-case classification uses the chosen side/angle values.

sections.heading: Parallelogram diagonal divides it into congruent triangles
paragraphs: Congruent triangle names encode correspondence: ΔABC≅ΔPQR matches A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R. Establish SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS or RHS before invoking corresponding parts of congruent triangles (CPCT). For a parallelogram ABCD, diagonal AC is shared and opposite sides match; SSS proves ΔABC≅ΔCDA, so the diagonal splits the shape into equal-area triangles.

A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles; a rhombus is a parallelogram with equal sides. A square satisfies both. Properties must not be confused with a picture that only looks like a special case: a diagram can suggest a claim, while congruence and angle reasoning prove it. State the given properties, identify which class they force, and justify each conclusion. In the tool a parallelogram is built from two sides and an included angle. Try equal sides, a right angle, or both; then compare the diagonals and area.
Remember: Equal sides gives rhombus; right angle gives rectangle; both gives square.

paragraphs: A rhombus must have right angles. Correction: Equal sides alone do not fix its angles. A non-square rhombus is a counterexample.

objectives: Explain equal chords and equal distances from the centre.

sections.heading: Equal chords and equal distances from the centre
paragraphs: Drop perpendiculars from centre O to two chords AB and CD. Each perpendicular bisects its chord by congruent right triangles. Equal chord halves and equal radii give equal perpendicular distances by Pythagoras. Conversely, equal distances with equal radii give equal chord halves. The comparison must be in the same circle or in circles of equal radii.
The perpendicular from a circle centre to a chord bisects it. Radius, perpendicular distance and half-chord form a right triangle.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Within one circle or equal-radius circles, equal chords have equal distances from the centre and conversely. Radius must be held fixed for that comparison. A longer chord sits closer to the centre; the diameter corresponds to distance zero.

Draw the perpendicular, label the radius and half-chord, then use Pythagoras. Double the half-chord to get the full length. If comparing circles, check their radii before transferring an equal-distance conclusion.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: The radii must also agree. The formula includes both r and d.
Recall cue: Half a chord joins the centre-distance right triangle.

sections.heading: Finding area from three sides

lessons.title: Grouped data and class intervals
lessons.summary: Grouped data record counts in intervals rather than the individual observations. Means, medians and modes calculated from such groups generally involve approximation.
objectives: Explain grouped data and class intervals.
Calculate and interpret total frequency, estimated mean using mean=Σfm/Σf; median=L+[(N/2−CF)/f]h.

sections.heading: Grouped data and class intervals
paragraphs: Grouped data record counts in intervals rather than the individual observations. Means, medians and modes calculated from such groups generally involve approximation. Build frequency and cumulative-frequency columns. For mean sum frequency times midpoint and divide by total. For median locate N/2 and interpolate using the previous cumulative count. For mode first identify a unique modal class and check the class-width assumptions.
Grouped data record counts in intervals rather than the individual observations. Means, medians and modes calculated from such groups generally involve approximation.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Class midpoints stand in for unknown values when finding a grouped mean. The median class contains the halfway cumulative count; interpolation assumes observations are spread within that interval. A grouped mode formula additionally uses neighbouring class frequencies and normally equal class widths.

Build frequency and cumulative-frequency columns. For mean sum frequency times midpoint and divide by total. For median locate N/2 and interpolate using the previous cumulative count. For mode first identify a unique modal class and check the class-width assumptions.

lessons.title: Histograms with unequal class widths
lessons.summary: A histogram represents continuous grouped data with adjoining rectangles. When class widths differ, frequency must be represented by area rather than raw height.
objectives: Explain histograms with unequal class widths.
Calculate and interpret first density, second density using frequency density=frequency/class width.
Recognize why this claim fails: The highest histogram rectangle must have the largest frequency.

sections.heading: Histograms with unequal class widths
paragraphs: A histogram represents continuous grouped data with adjoining rectangles. When class widths differ, frequency must be represented by area rather than raw height. Inspect class widths before choosing a vertical scale. Calculate density for every class, draw the interval width on the horizontal axis and density on the vertical axis, then verify width times height recovers the count. Label the scale clearly.
A histogram represents continuous grouped data with adjoining rectangles. When class widths differ, frequency must be represented by area rather than raw height.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Frequency density equals frequency divided by width. A wider interval with the same frequency needs a lower rectangle so its area remains equal to that frequency. The usual raw-frequency height is suitable only under a common-width convention.

Inspect class widths before choosing a vertical scale. Calculate density for every class, draw the interval width on the horizontal axis and density on the vertical axis, then verify width times height recovers the count. Label the scale clearly.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Class midpoints stand in for unknown values when finding a grouped mean. lessons.title: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic and uniqueness
lessons.summary: The highest common factor is the greatest positive divisor shared by two positive integers. The least common multiple is their smallest positive common multiple.
objectives: Explain fundamental theorem of arithmetic and uniqueness.
Calculate and interpret hcf, lcm using HCF(a,b)×LCM(a,b)=ab.

sections.heading: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic and uniqueness
paragraphs: The highest common factor is the greatest positive divisor shared by two positive integers. The least common multiple is their smallest positive common multiple. Identify whether the problem concerns common grouping or a common repeat. Calculate HCF, then LCM=ab/HCF. Check both divisibility conditions and the product identity. The two-number identity should not be transferred unchanged to three numbers.
The highest common factor is the greatest positive divisor shared by two positive integers. The least common multiple is their smallest positive common multiple.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Prime factorizations give HCF by taking minimum exponents and LCM by maximum exponents. For two positive integers their product equals HCF times LCM. Equal-group packing suggests HCF; coinciding repeating events suggest LCM.

lessons.title: Proof by contradiction for irrational square roots
lessons.summary: A nonnegative number can be located between consecutive perfect squares to bound its square root.
objectives: Explain proof by contradiction for irrational square roots.

sections.heading: Proof by contradiction for irrational square roots
paragraphs: Suppose √2=p/q in lowest positive integer terms. Squaring gives p²=2q², hence p is even; write p=2k. Then q²=2k², so q is even too, contradicting that p/q was reduced. Numerical root bounds locate √2 but cannot establish its irrationality. For general nonsquare positive integers, use odd prime exponents in a parallel factorisation argument.
A nonnegative number can be located between consecutive perfect squares to bound its square root.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Squaring preserves order for nonnegative values. Thus 7²<60<8² implies 7<√60<8. A decimal approximation is useful but remains different from an exact value or a proven interval.
List nearby squares and find the bounding pair. Refine with tenths if needed by squaring the trial values. Label every rounded answer as approximate and check its square against the original number.

lessons.title: Rational/irrational combinations and proofs
lessons.summary: Between two distinct rational numbers there is another rational number, and this construction can be repeated indefinitely. Irrational numbers also occur in every such interval.
objectives: Explain rational/irrational combinations and proofs.
Calculate and interpret rational midpoint, approximate irrational point using midpoint=(a+b)/2.
Recognize why this claim fails: A nonterminating-looking calculator display proves irrationality.

sections.heading: Rational/irrational combinations and proofs
paragraphs: A nonzero rational multiplied by an irrational is irrational: otherwise division by that rational would make the original irrational rational. A rational plus an irrational is irrational by subtraction. Two irrationals can sum to a rational (√2+(−√2)=0) or an irrational (√2+√2), so there is no universal closure claim for their sums.
Between two distinct rational numbers there is another rational number, and this construction can be repeated indefinitely. Irrational numbers also occur in every such interval.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The average of two rational endpoints is rational and lies strictly inside. For rational a<b, a+(b−a)/√2 is irrational and also inside because 0<1/√2<1. Displayed finite decimals approximate the latter; the formula establishes its irrationality.

Order the endpoints. Construct their average and verify both inequalities. Repeat on a subinterval to obtain more rationals. For an irrational example use an exact irrational expression, not a finite decimal claimed to be irrational.

sections.heading: Rational/irrational combinations and proofs
paragraphs: A nonzero rational multiplied by an irrational is irrational: otherwise division by that rational would make the original irrational rational. A rational plus an irrational is irrational by subtraction. Two irrationals can sum to a rational (√2+(−√2)=0) or an irrational (√2+√2), so there is no universal closure claim for their sums.

Repeat on a subinterval to obtain more rationals. For an irrational example use an exact irrational expression, not a finite decimal claimed to be irrational.
Remember: Midpoint gives a rational; an exact irrational shift gives another kind.

formulas.meaning: Prime factorizations give HCF by taking minimum exponents and LCM by maximum exponents. For two positive integers their product equals HCF times LCM. Equal-group packing suggests HCF; coinciding repeating events suggest LCM.
formulas.restriction: Two positive integers only.

formulas.meaning: Squaring preserves order for nonnegative values. Thus 7²<60<8² implies 7<√60<8. A decimal approximation is useful but remains different from an exact value or a proven interval.
formulas.restriction: This order argument applies to real x≥0 and nonnegative comparison values.

formulas.meaning: The average of two rational endpoints is rational and lies strictly inside. For rational a<b, a+(b−a)/√2 is irrational and also inside because 0<1/√2<1. Displayed finite decimals approximate the latter; the formula establishes its irrationality.
formulas.restriction: This demonstration uses rational endpoints represented by integers; a<b is required.

misconceptions.mistake: HCF and LCM are interchangeable in word problems.
misconceptions.correction: They solve different grouping/repetition questions. Read what must divide or be divided by the result.

misconceptions.mistake: √50 is exactly 7.1.
misconceptions.correction: 7.1²=50.41, so 7.1 is an upper bound here, not the exact root.

misconceptions.mistake: A nonterminating-looking calculator display proves irrationality.
misconceptions.correction: A finite display is rational. Irrationality belongs to the exact number and needs an argument.

sections.heading: Zeros of quadratic/cubic polynomials from graphs
paragraphs: Zeros are x-values with p(x)=0, so a graph zero is a meeting with the x-axis, including tangency. A monic quadratic with zeros r and s is (x−r)(x−s)=x²−(r+s)x+rs. sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: For x²+sx+p, candidate constants a,b need both a+b=s and ab=p. One condition alone is insufficient. Regrouping also uses common factors: ax+ay+bx+by=a(x+y)+b(x+y)=(a+b)(x+y). A zero of a factored polynomial makes at least one factor zero.

sections.heading: Elimination method

lessons.title: Solving quadratics by factorisation
lessons.summary: A quadratic equation ax²+bx+c=0 has a nonzero leading coefficient. Its discriminant D=b²−4ac determines the number of distinct real roots.
objectives: Explain solving quadratics by factorisation.
Calculate and interpret root 1, root 2, discriminant using D=b²−4ac; x=(−b±√D)/(2a).
Recognize why this claim fails: D=0 means zero is the root.

sections.heading: Solving quadratics by factorisation
paragraphs: Put the equation in ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0. Factoring uses the zero-product property; completing the square yields x=(−b±√(b²−4ac))/(2a). A negative discriminant gives two conjugate complex roots but no real roots. A repeated real root has multiplicity two. In a length or time problem, substitute every algebraic candidate into the original context and reject negative or otherwise inadmissible values.
A quadratic equation ax²+bx+c=0 has a nonzero leading coefficient. Its discriminant D=b²−4ac determines the number of distinct real roots.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: D>0 gives two distinct real roots; D=0 gives one repeated root; D<0 gives no real roots. A polynomial zero is an input giving output zero. The zero-sum and zero-product relations connect roots to coefficients and help construct a polynomial from known roots.

Identify a,b,c with signs, calculate D, and state the real-root case. Factor when possible or use the quadratic formula. Substitute each root into the original equation. In a context problem reject roots incompatible with the meaning, such as a negative physical length.

paragraphs: It means the two formula branches agree. For x²+4x+4, the repeated root is −2.

lessons.title: Nth term of an arithmetic progression
lessons.summary: An arithmetic progression adds the same common difference at every step. The nth term lies n−1 steps after the first term.
objectives: Explain nth term of an arithmetic progression.
Calculate and interpret nth term using aₙ=a+(n−1)d; Sₙ=n[2a+(n−1)d]/2.
Recognize why this claim fails: Use a+nd for the nth term.

sections.heading: Nth term of an arithmetic progression
paragraphs: An arithmetic progression adds the same common difference at every step. The nth term lies n−1 steps after the first term. Identify the first term a and difference d. Use a+(n−1)d for a position query. For a sum compute the last term, then n times the average of first and last. If solving for n, require a positive integer and check the term really occurs.
An arithmetic progression adds the same common difference at every step. The nth term lies n−1 steps after the first term.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The sum of the first n terms can be found by pairing the first with the last, the second with the next-to-last and so on. Every such pair has the same total. An increasing sequence is not necessarily arithmetic: its consecutive differences must agree.

Identify the first term a and difference d. Use a+(n−1)d for a position query. For a sum compute the last term, then n times the average of first and last. If solving for n, require a positive integer and check the term really occurs.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: That takes n steps instead of n−1. For n=1, the formula must return a.
Recall cue: Nth term has n−1 gaps; sum is count times end-average.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: The first term precedes n−1 gaps. Each gap adds d, so the nth term is a+(n−1)d. Pairing first and last terms explains the sum formula.
For the initial values, Nth term = 19; Sum = 55. aₙ=a+(n−1)d; Sₙ=n[2a+(n−1)d]/2

sections.heading: Finding missing terms and term positions
paragraphs: For an AP, solve n=1+(t−a)/d when d≠0. A requested term exists only if this result is a positive integer. When d=0, all terms equal a and no unique position is determined. To insert m terms between endpoints A and B, divide B−A by m+1 because that is the number of gaps.

lessons.title: Basic proportionality theorem with proof
lessons.summary: A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio. The converse can establish parallelism from equality of those ratios.
objectives: Explain basic proportionality theorem with proof.
Calculate and interpret ec, ad/ab, ae/ac using AD/DB=AE/EC.
Recognize why this claim fails: Use AD/DB=AE/AC.

sections.heading: Basic proportionality theorem with proof
paragraphs: For DE parallel to BC in ΔABC with D on AB and E on AC, triangles BDE and CDE have equal areas because they share base DE and lie between parallels. Comparing areas of ADE with BDE gives AD/DB, and with CDE gives AE/EC. Equality of the denominators yields AD/DB=AE/EC. This proves the basic proportionality theorem without treating a measured drawing as proof.
A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio. The converse can establish parallelism from equality of those ratios.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: One proof compares areas of triangles sharing heights or bases, then uses equal-altitude triangles on the parallel lines. Another formulation uses similar triangles. The forward theorem requires the parallel premise; the converse begins with proportional divisions. A drawn parallel-looking segment is not the premise.

Label the four side segments in the same direction. Write AD/DB=AE/EC and solve by cross multiplication. For a converse problem check both ratios, then state why the line is parallel. Do not replace a side segment with the whole side accidentally.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: The denominators must correspond. Split-to-split ratios and part-to-whole ratios are different but each can be consistent.
Recall cue: Parallel cut gives equal splits; equal splits can prove parallel cut.

sections.heading: Basic proportionality theorem with proof
paragraphs: For DE parallel to BC in ΔABC with D on AB and E on AC, triangles BDE and CDE have equal areas because they share base DE and lie between parallels. Comparing areas of ADE with BDE gives AD/DB, and with CDE gives AE/EC. Equality of the denominators yields AD/DB=AE/EC. This proves the basic proportionality theorem without treating a measured drawing as proof.

One proof compares areas of triangles sharing heights or bases, then uses equal-altitude triangles on the parallel lines. Another formulation uses similar triangles. The forward theorem requires the parallel premise; the converse begins with proportional divisions. A drawn parallel-looking segment is not the premise. Label the four side segments in the same direction. Write AD/DB=AE/EC and solve by cross multiplication. For a converse problem check both ratios, then state why the line is parallel. Do not replace a side segment with the whole side accidentally.
Remember: Parallel cut gives equal splits; equal splits can prove parallel cut.

sections.heading: Converse of basic proportionality theorem
paragraphs: Given AD/DB=AE/EC for interior points, draw through D a line parallel to BC meeting AC at E′. BPT gives AD/DB=AE′/E′C. The same total side AC forces E′=E, so DE is parallel to BC. Positivity and the requirement that the points lie on the triangle sides matter.

sections.heading: Basic proportionality theorem with proof
paragraphs: For DE parallel to BC in ΔABC with D on AB and E on AC, triangles BDE and CDE have equal areas because they share base DE and lie between parallels. Comparing areas of ADE with BDE gives AD/DB, and with CDE gives AE/EC. Equality of the denominators yields AD/DB=AE/EC. This proves the basic proportionality theorem without treating a measured drawing as proof.

One proof compares areas of triangles sharing heights or bases, then uses equal-altitude triangles on the parallel lines. Another formulation uses similar triangles. The forward theorem requires the parallel premise; the converse begins with proportional divisions. A drawn parallel-looking segment is not the premise. Label the four side segments in the same direction. Write AD/DB=AE/EC and solve by cross multiplication. For a converse problem check both ratios, then state why the line is parallel. Do not replace a side segment with the whole side accidentally.
Remember: Parallel cut gives equal splits; equal splits can prove parallel cut.

sections.heading: Converse of basic proportionality theorem
paragraphs: Given AD/DB=AE/EC for interior points, draw through D a line parallel to BC meeting AC at E′. BPT gives AD/DB=AE′/E′C. The same total side AC forces E′=E, so DE is parallel to BC. Positivity and the requirement that the points lie on the triangle sides matter.

sections.heading: Checking collinearity and classifying figures by distances
paragraphs: For A(x₁,y₁), B(x₂,y₂), C(x₃,y₃), collinearity means (x₂−x₁)(y₃−y₁)−(y₂−y₁)(x₃−x₁)=0. This handles vertical lines without slope division. sections.heading: Why the method works

lessons.title: Opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse conventions
lessons.summary: In a right triangle, sine is opposite/hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent/hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite/adjacent relative to a chosen acute angle.
objectives: Explain opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse conventions.
Calculate and interpret sine, cosine, tangent, cosecant, secant, cotangent using sin²θ+cos²θ=1.
Recognize why this claim fails: The opposite side stays the same when the reference angle changes.

sections.heading: Opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse conventions
paragraphs: Relative to θ in a right triangle, opposite changes if you choose the other acute angle, while the hypotenuse stays opposite the right angle. SOH-CAH-TOA gives sine, cosine and tangent; reciprocals give cosecant, secant and cotangent where denominators are nonzero. At 30°, (sin,cos)=(1/2,√3/2); at 45°, both are 1/√2; at 60°, they swap. Squaring opposite²+adjacent²=hypotenuse² proves sin²θ+cos²θ=1.
In a right triangle, sine is opposite/hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent/hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite/adjacent relative to a chosen acute angle.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Similar right triangles explain why the ratios depend on the angle rather than the overall size. Pythagoras divided by hypotenuse² gives sin²θ+cos²θ=1. Reciprocal ratios require nonzero denominators. At endpoint angles some ratios are undefined, so the tool reports that rather than a huge misleading number.

Choose the reference angle before naming opposite and adjacent sides. Select the ratio that uses the known and requested sides. Keep degree units explicit. For exact special angles use the 30–60–90 or 45–45–90 triangle values, distinguishing those from rounded decimals.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: Switching between the two acute angles swaps opposite and adjacent. The hypotenuse stays opposite the right angle.
Recall cue: SOH-CAH-TOA; reference angle first.

lessons.title: Tangent, secant and point of contact
lessons.summary: A tangent touches a circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that contact point. An external point has two tangent segments of equal length.
objectives: Explain tangent, secant and point of contact.
Calculate and interpret number of tangents using PT²=OP²−r² for an external point.
Recognize why this claim fails: Every point determines two tangents.

sections.heading: Tangent, secant and point of contact
paragraphs: A tangent meets the circle at one point; a secant crosses it at two. The radius to a point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. An exterior point has two equal tangent segments: their right triangles share the centre-to-point hypotenuse and have equal radii, so RHS proves equality. A point on the circle has one tangent line, even though the tangent-segment length measured from that point is zero.
A tangent touches a circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that contact point. An external point has two tangent segments of equal length.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The radius and tangent segment form a right triangle with the centre-to-external-point distance as hypotenuse. An inside point has no real tangent; a point on the circle has one tangent line. Counting tangent lines is different from treating the zero-length on-circle segment as an external construction.

Compare OP with radius r first. For an external point compute √(OP²−r²). Use the equal-tangent theorem for other lengths, and use the radius perpendicularity only at the actual contact point. Verify the radicand is nonnegative.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: Inside gives none, on-circle gives one line, and outside gives two. Location must be checked first.
Recall cue: Radius is perpendicular at contact; external tangents have equal lengths.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: From an exterior point, the tangent segment and radius form a right triangle. The hypotenuse is the centre-to-point distance; no real tangent segment exists from an interior point.
For the initial values, Number of tangents = 2; Tangent length = 4. PT²=OP²−r² for an external point

sections.heading: Tangent, secant and point of contact
paragraphs: A tangent meets the circle at one point; a secant crosses it at two. The radius to a point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. An exterior point has two equal tangent segments: their right triangles share the centre-to-point hypotenuse and have equal radii, so RHS proves equality. A point on the circle has one tangent line, even though the tangent-segment length measured from that point is zero.

Use the equal-tangent theorem for other lengths, and use the radius perpendicularity only at the actual contact point. Verify the radicand is nonnegative.
Remember: Radius is perpendicular at contact; external tangents have equal lengths.

sections.heading: Exposed versus joined surfaces of composite solids
paragraphs: Draw each component and mark the joined faces. A cone on a hemisphere shares a disk that is internal; exposed area includes cone curved area plus hemisphere curved area. objectives: Explain grouped-data approximation and class marks.
