sections.heading: Grouped-data approximation and class marks
paragraphs: Grouped data record counts in intervals rather than the individual observations. Means, medians and modes calculated from such groups generally involve approximation. Build frequency and cumulative-frequency columns. For mean sum frequency times midpoint and divide by total. For median locate N/2 and interpolate using the previous cumulative count. For mode first identify a unique modal class and check the class-width assumptions.
Grouped data record counts in intervals rather than the individual observations. Means, medians and modes calculated from such groups generally involve approximation.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Class midpoints stand in for unknown values when finding a grouped mean. The median class contains the halfway cumulative count; interpolation assumes observations are spread within that interval. A grouped mode formula additionally uses neighbouring class frequencies and normally equal class widths.

lessons.title: Modal class and grouped-mode formula
lessons.summary: Grouped data record counts in intervals rather than the individual observations. Means, medians and modes calculated from such groups generally involve approximation.
objectives: Explain modal class and grouped-mode formula.
Calculate and interpret middle-class mode estimate using mean=Σfm/Σf; median=L+[(N/2−CF)/f]h.
Recognize why this claim fails: Grouped means recover the exact mean of the unknown raw data.

sections.heading: Modal class and grouped-mode formula
paragraphs: For a uniquely modal interior class, mode=L+[(f₁−f₀)/(2f₁−f₀−f₂)]h. For the median class, median=L+[(N/2−CF)/f]h, where CF excludes that class. Grouped mean uses class midpoints and is an estimate. These three centres can differ for skewed data; the empirical mean-mode relation is an approximation, not an identity. The tool supports three equal-width classes, with mode interpolation only for a uniquely modal middle class.

lessons.title: Equally likely outcomes and theoretical probability
lessons.summary: The classical counting formula P(E)=favourable/total requires a finite sample space of equally likely outcomes.
objectives: Explain equally likely outcomes and theoretical probability.
Calculate and interpret event probability using P(E)=favourable/total.
Recognize why this claim fails: Every listed outcome has equal probability automatically.

sections.heading: Equally likely outcomes and theoretical probability
paragraphs: The classical counting formula P(E)=favourable/total requires a finite sample space of equally likely outcomes. List or count outcomes systematically, check equal likelihood, count the event outcomes, and form the fraction. For a complement count the remaining outcomes or subtract from 1. If outcomes have unequal weights, add their probabilities instead of counting them equally.
The classical counting formula P(E)=favourable/total requires a finite sample space of equally likely outcomes.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The probability of an impossible event is 0 and of a certain event is 1. Every probability lies between them. An event and its complement partition the entire sample space, giving probabilities that add to 1. “Favourable” means meeting the specified event, not a value judgment.

List or count outcomes systematically, check equal likelihood, count the event outcomes, and form the fraction. For a complement count the remaining outcomes or subtract from 1. If outcomes have unequal weights, add their probabilities instead of counting them equally.

sections.heading: Listing sample spaces systematically
paragraphs: Repeated fair independent coin tosses produce ordered outcomes. For k tosses there are 2ᵏ equally likely strings of heads and tails. List both branches at each toss and keep the order. sections.heading: Why the method works

objectives: Explain multiplying two or more monomials.

sections.heading: Multiplying two or more monomials
paragraphs: A monomial is a single product of a coefficient and nonnegative integer variable powers. Multiplying monomials multiplies coefficients and adds exponents for each common variable. lessons.title: Nets and recognition of solid shapes
lessons.summary: A cuboid has three pairs of equal opposite rectangular faces. Surface area adds the six faces; volume multiplies its three perpendicular dimensions.
objectives: Explain nets and recognition of solid shapes.
Calculate and interpret surface area using SA=2(ab+bh+ha); V=abh.
Recognize why this claim fails: Convert square centimetres to litres.

sections.heading: Nets and recognition of solid shapes
paragraphs: Decompose a polygon into nonoverlapping rectangles, triangles or trapezia and sum their areas; subtract holes separately. A cuboid net has three opposite pairs of rectangular faces. A cube has six congruent square faces, so SA=6s² and V=s³. A drawn net must fold without overlapping faces: merely having six squares does not ensure a valid cube net.
A cuboid has three pairs of equal opposite rectangular faces. Surface area adds the six faces; volume multiplies its three perpendicular dimensions.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Area and volume measure different quantities. A net unfolds the surface into rectangles, while a stack of unit cubes explains volume. Capacity can be expressed in litres: 1000 cm³ equals 1 litre, but 1000 cm² is not a capacity unit.

Put all dimensions in the same length unit. Compute ab, bh and ha for face areas, double their sum for total area, and multiply abh for volume. For a cube set all dimensions equal, reducing the formulas to 6s² and s³.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: Litres measure volume. Use cubic centimetres and the volume conversion factor.
Recall cue: Three face areas twice; three lengths multiplied.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: Lengths define the solid, areas measure surfaces, and volumes measure filled space. Scaling every length by k scales area by k² and volume by k³. Joined internal faces do not contribute to exposed area.

sections.heading: Cube surface area
paragraphs: Decompose a polygon into nonoverlapping rectangles, triangles or trapezia and sum their areas; subtract holes separately. A cuboid net has three opposite pairs of rectangular faces. lessons.summary: A negative exponent means a reciprocal: b⁻ⁿ=1/bⁿ for a nonzero base. It does not automatically mean a negative answer.
objectives: Explain negative-exponent meaning and evaluation.

sections.heading: Negative-exponent meaning and evaluation
paragraphs: A negative exponent means a reciprocal: b⁻ⁿ=1/bⁿ for a nonzero base. It does not automatically mean a negative answer. Evaluate the positive power in the denominator, then invert. For a fractional base, inversion also swaps numerator and denominator. Keep parentheses around a negative or fractional base.
A negative exponent means a reciprocal: b⁻ⁿ=1/bⁿ for a nonzero base. It does not automatically mean a negative answer.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The product bⁿb⁻ⁿ must equal b⁰=1. Therefore b⁻ⁿ is the number that multiplies bⁿ to give 1. The sign of the base and the parity of an integer exponent determine the sign separately.

sections.heading: Scientific notation for small numbers
paragraphs: Powers of ten describe decimal place value: multiplying by 10ᵉ scales the value by a factor of ten e times when e is positive. Locate the units position. Powers of ten describe decimal place value: multiplying by 10ᵉ scales the value by a factor of ten e times when e is positive.

sections.heading: Why the method works

objectives: Explain comparing large and small quantities.

Recognize why this claim fails: The bigger coefficient always gives the bigger value.

sections.heading: Comparing large and small quantities
paragraphs: To compare positive numbers in normalized scientific notation, compare exponents first and coefficients second. Confirm each expression is normalized and positive. Compare its exponent. If the exponents agree, compare coefficients; otherwise the greater exponent gives the larger number. For a ratio, divide coefficients and subtract exponents.
To compare positive numbers in normalized scientific notation, compare exponents first and coefficients second.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Coefficients between 1 and 10 cannot outweigh a whole exponent step: 9.9×10⁴ is smaller than 1.1×10⁵. If exponents match, ordinary coefficient order decides. Negative values require attention to sign before magnitude.

Confirm each expression is normalized and positive. Compare its exponent. If the exponents agree, compare coefficients; otherwise the greater exponent gives the larger number. For a ratio, divide coefficients and subtract exponents.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer

sections.heading: Direct-proportion contextual problems
paragraphs: A ratio compares quantities multiplicatively and preserves their order. Dividing both terms by the same positive factor produces an equivalent ratio. sections.heading: Work, time and sharing inverse-proportion problems
paragraphs: Inverse proportion keeps a product constant. If the same work is done by twice as many equally productive workers, the idealised time halves. Calculate the original product of workers and time. Divide that workload by the new worker count. Check the new product equals the old product and explain whether the assumptions fit the real situation.
Inverse proportion keeps a product constant. If the same work is done by twice as many equally productive workers, the idealised time halves.

sections.heading: Why the method works

sections.heading: Factors of numbers and algebraic expressions
paragraphs: Factorisation reverses expansion: a polynomial is expressed as a product whose multiplication recreates it. Look for a common factor first, then use an identity or two-number sum/product search. Expand your proposed factors to check every coefficient. Factorisation reverses expansion: a polynomial is expressed as a product whose multiplication recreates it.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: For x²+sx+p, candidate constants a,b need both a+b=s and ab=p. One condition alone is insufficient. Regrouping also uses common factors: ax+ay+bx+by=a(x+y)+b(x+y)=(a+b)(x+y). A zero of a factored polynomial makes at least one factor zero.

lessons.title: Reading and constructing line graphs
lessons.summary: A line graph connects values in an ordered quantitative sequence. For a constant-rate model y=mx+k, slope m measures output change per input unit.
objectives: Explain reading and constructing line graphs.
Calculate and interpret slope, intercept, output using y=mx+k.
Recognize why this claim fails: A graph higher up must represent a faster change.

sections.heading: Reading and constructing line graphs
paragraphs: A line graph connects values in an ordered quantitative sequence. For a constant-rate model y=mx+k, slope m measures output change per input unit. Label both axes and units, choose an even scale, plot ordered pairs, and interpret the change between points. For this affine model read the intercept at zero and compute rise/run for its rate. Explain whether interpolation between observations is justified.
A line graph connects values in an ordered quantitative sequence. For a constant-rate model y=mx+k, slope m measures output change per input unit.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Position on a graph and rate are different. A high position does not mean a high slope. In distance-time contexts the slope has units of distance/time, and a fixed initial value shifts the graph without changing that constant rate. Discrete or discontinuous data should not be connected indiscriminately.

Label both axes and units, choose an even scale, plot ordered pairs, and interpret the change between points. For this affine model read the intercept at zero and compute rise/run for its rate. Explain whether interpolation between observations is justified.

lessons.title: Coordinates and plotting points on a grid
lessons.summary: An ordered pair (x,y) locates a point by horizontal movement first and vertical movement second. The order carries meaning.
objectives: Explain coordinates and plotting points on a grid.
Calculate and interpret x-coordinate, y-coordinate, location using P=(x,y).
Recognize why this claim fails: Every point belongs to one of the four quadrants.

sections.heading: Coordinates and plotting points on a grid
paragraphs: An ordered pair (x,y) locates a point by horizontal movement first and vertical movement second. The order carries meaning. Start at the origin. Move horizontally by x, then vertically by y. Read the coordinates in that same order. Use a common scale and labelled axes when describing a map; interchanging coordinates usually changes the point.
An ordered pair (x,y) locates a point by horizontal movement first and vertical movement second. The order carries meaning.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The horizontal axis is the x-axis; the vertical axis is the y-axis. Signs identify quadrants away from the axes. A point with x=0 lies on the y-axis, and a point with y=0 lies on the x-axis; neither belongs to a quadrant.

Start at the origin. Move horizontally by x, then vertically by y. Read the coordinates in that same order. Use a common scale and labelled axes when describing a map; interchanging coordinates usually changes the point.

objectives: Explain readiness: factors, primes, squares and cubes.

sections.heading: Readiness: factors, primes, squares and cubes
paragraphs: The highest common factor is the greatest positive divisor shared by two positive integers. The least common multiple is their smallest positive common multiple. Identify whether the problem concerns common grouping or a common repeat. Calculate HCF, then LCM=ab/HCF. Check both divisibility conditions and the product identity. The two-number identity should not be transferred unchanged to three numbers.

sections.heading: Why the method works

objectives: Explain readiness: number representations and place value.

sections.heading: Readiness: number representations and place value
paragraphs: Indian large-number names group places as ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, lakhs and crores. One lakh is 100000 and one crore is 10000000. Read the place groups from the right. Convert a named quantity to its underlying number before arithmetic. Divide by 100000 for lakhs or 10000000 for crores. Reconstruct the number to check a conversion.
Indian large-number names group places as ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, lakhs and crores. One lakh is 100000 and one crore is 10000000.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The numerical value is independent of the comma convention. Indian grouping keeps the final three digits together and groups the remaining digits in pairs. Place-value notation uses zero to hold empty places so 1005 differs from 105.

sections.heading: Why the method works

lessons.title: Square-number patterns and the locker puzzle
lessons.summary: A positive integer is a perfect square exactly when every exponent in its prime factorisation is even.
objectives: Explain square-number patterns and the locker puzzle.
Calculate and interpret positive divisor count, perfect square? using d(n) = ∏(eᵢ + 1).
Recognize why this claim fails: Every number ending in 1 is square.

sections.heading: Square-number patterns and the locker puzzle
paragraphs: Locker k is toggled once for every positive divisor of k. Divisors usually pair as d and k/d; only a square has an unpaired middle divisor √k. Thus exactly the square-numbered lockers have an odd number of toggles and finish open when all start closed. For 100 lockers, those numbers are 1² through 10².
A positive integer is a perfect square exactly when every exponent in its prime factorisation is even.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Each prime factor of a square comes from multiplying two identical factorisations. Positive divisors pair as d and n/d; only the square root pairs with itself. Therefore perfect squares have an odd number of positive divisors.

Write n as a product of prime powers. Check each exponent for evenness. A last digit of 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 is possible for a square, but is only a quick screening test: 26 ends in 6 and is not square.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: Ending in 1 is necessary for some squares, not sufficient. For example, 21 is not a square.
Recall cue: Even prime exponents make a square; an allowed last digit only makes a candidate.

sections.heading: Read the visualization

objectives: Explain exponential growth in computational processes.

sections.heading: Exponential growth in computational processes
paragraphs: Use mathematical rules to inspect a computational output: define inputs, trace each operation, and independently check a small example. Repeated doubling is multiplicative growth: each stage multiplies the current amount by 2. After n stages, the amount is Q₀2ⁿ.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: The stage counter begins at zero with the starting amount. Adding 2 each stage makes linear growth, a different process. In a paper-folding model, the thickness formula is idealised: real paper cannot be folded arbitrarily many times.
Record the initial amount. Multiply by 2 once for each stage, or use 2ⁿ to combine the repeated factors. Check n=0 before interpreting the table so the first doubling is not counted twice.

lessons.title: Positional notation and representing digital data
lessons.summary: A positional system gives a digit its value from both its symbol and its position. In base b the places are 1, b, b², b³ and so on.
objectives: Explain positional notation and representing digital data.
Calculate and interpret representation, base, decimal value using N = Σ digit × base^position.
Recognize why this claim fails: Every numeral system uses exactly the same place weights.

sections.heading: Positional notation and representing digital data
paragraphs: Use mathematical rules to inspect a computational output: define inputs, trace each operation, and independently check a small example. A classifier based on shape properties needs inclusive categories, and a balanced dataset ratio does not by itself establish fairness. AI explanations can contain incorrect arithmetic or unstated assumptions; verify them against calculations and sources before using them as teaching evidence.
A positional system gives a digit its value from both its symbol and its position. In base b the places are 1, b, b², b³ and so on.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Only digits 0 through b−1 are allowed. A zero digit holds an empty place: 101 in base 2 means one four, zero twos and one unit. Without its position, a digit alone cannot tell the full contribution.

To decode, multiply each digit by its place weight and add. To encode a nonnegative integer, repeatedly divide by the base and read the remainders backwards. Check by converting the representation back to the original number.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: Egyptian additive notation and calendar-style Mayan weights illustrate why the convention must be stated.

sections.heading: Read the visualization

lessons.title: Quadrilateral features and shape classification
lessons.summary: Quadrilaterals are closed figures with four straight sides. Particular side, angle and diagonal conditions identify special classes.
objectives: Explain quadrilateral features and shape classification.

sections.heading: Quadrilateral features and shape classification
paragraphs: Use inclusive definitions: every square belongs to the rectangles and to the rhombi, and both are parallelograms. A property is necessary when every member has it; it is sufficient when it forces membership. Equal diagonals are necessary for rectangles but insufficient among arbitrary quadrilaterals. Classify by stated properties rather than visual orientation.
Quadrilaterals are closed figures with four straight sides. Particular side, angle and diagonal conditions identify special classes.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles; a rhombus is a parallelogram with equal sides. A square satisfies both. Properties must not be confused with a picture that only looks like a special case: a diagram can suggest a claim, while congruence and angle reasoning prove it.

State the given properties, identify which class they force, and justify each conclusion. In the tool a parallelogram is built from two sides and an included angle. Try equal sides, a right angle, or both; then compare the diagonals and area.

The distributive law multiplies every term inside a bracket by the outside factor: a(b+c)=ab+ac.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: An area split into two adjoining rectangles gives the same total as the unsplit rectangle when lengths are nonnegative. The algebraic identity also works for signed numbers. Using it for subtraction means distributing the minus sign or negative factor to every term.

lessons.title: Statements, conjectures, counterexamples and mathematical proofs
lessons.summary: Even integers have form 2k, and odd integers have form 2k+1. These algebraic forms explain sum and product parity rules.
objectives: Explain statements, conjectures, counterexamples and mathematical proofs.
Calculate and interpret sum parity, product parity, sum, product using even=2k; odd=2k+1.
Recognize why this claim fails: A collection of examples proves a parity rule.

sections.heading: Statements, conjectures, counterexamples and mathematical proofs
paragraphs: For arbitrary integers p and q, (2p+1)+(2q+1)=2(p+q+1), so odd+odd is always even. One counterexample disproves a universal claim: 3+5=8 disproves odd+odd is odd. A list of successful examples cannot prove a universal statement. A direct proof starts from definitions; contradiction assumes the negation and derives an impossibility.
Even integers have form 2k, and odd integers have form 2k+1. These algebraic forms explain sum and product parity rules.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: Even+even and odd+odd are even; even+odd is odd. A product with an even factor is even. Two odd factors multiply to an odd result because (2p+1)(2q+1)=2(2pq+p+q)+1. Checking examples helps find a rule but does not prove it for every integer.

Identify the parity of each input. Write its 2k or 2k+1 form and expand. Separate a factor of 2 from any leftover 1. Compare the tool output with this general proof, including zero as an even integer.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: Use algebra to cover arbitrary integers; use a counterexample to disprove an overly broad claim.
Recall cue: Even has no leftover after twos; odd has one.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: even=2k; odd=2k+1. 7 is odd and 9 is odd. Their sum is 16; product is 63. Algebraic forms 2k and 2k+1 establish the general rules; the displayed pair is an example.

formulas.meaning: Even+even and odd+odd are even; even+odd is odd. A product with an even factor is even. Two odd factors multiply to an odd result because (2p+1)(2q+1)=2(2pq+p+q)+1. Checking examples helps find a rule but does not prove it for every integer.

lessons.title: Theory of equations and reciprocal equations
lessons.summary: Reciprocal equations have coefficients symmetric from the leading term to the constant term. Their nonzero roots occur in reciprocal pairs because replacing x by 1/x reverses the polynomial.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain theory of equations and reciprocal equations.
Calculate and interpret reduced discriminant, reduced root sum, reduced root product using x⁴−ax³+bx²−ax+1=0 → t²−at+b−2=0, t=x+1/x.
Recognize why this claim fails: Every real reduced t gives real x roots.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: Reciprocal equations have coefficients symmetric from the leading term to the constant term. Their nonzero roots occur in reciprocal pairs because replacing x by 1/x reverses the polynomial.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Divide a reciprocal quartic by x², group x+1/x as t, and use x²+1/x²=t²−2. Solve for t first, then solve x²−tx+1=0 for each candidate. Check the original polynomial and count multiplicities.
The constant 1 excludes x=0, so division by x² is valid.
x²+1/x²=t²−2 gives the reduced quadratic.
Reduced discriminant=9; each real t yields real reciprocal x roots only if |t|≥2.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: Vieta relations follow by expanding a∏(x−rᵢ): the elementary symmetric root sums equal signed coefficient ratios. A repeated root can be detected by a common factor of p and p′. Reciprocal symmetry may involve plus or minus conventions; identify the actual coefficient pattern before substituting.
Real x requires t²−4≥0 as well; real t alone is insufficient.

sections.heading: Recall and explain
paragraphs: Memory cue: Reduce degree before solving roots.

sections.heading: Read the visualization

lessons.title: Translation and rotation of coordinate axes
lessons.summary: Changing coordinate axes changes the numerical description of a fixed point. Translation changes the origin; an orthonormal rotation changes the directions without changing lengths or angles.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain translation and rotation of coordinate axes.
Calculate and interpret new x, new y, squared distance using x'=x cosθ+y sinθ; y'=−x sinθ+y cosθ.
Recognize why this claim fails: Rotating the axes and rotating the point use identical coordinate formulas.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: Changing coordinate axes changes the numerical description of a fixed point. Translation changes the origin; an orthonormal rotation changes the directions without changing lengths or angles.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: For an origin shifted to (h,k), use x′=x−h and y′=y−k. For a passive counterclockwise axis rotation, project onto the new axes: x′=x cosθ+y sinθ and y′=−x sinθ+y cosθ. Substitute these relations into the equation of a curve.
Rotate the axes counterclockwise by 30°, keeping the physical point fixed.
Project old point (3,4) onto the new unit axes.
The squared distance from the origin remains 25.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: For a conic Ax²+Bxy+Cy²+Dx+Ey+F=0, an appropriate rotation can remove the mixed term. A translation can then centre suitable conics. Active rotation of the point uses the opposite sign convention, so label the transformation carefully.
An active point rotation and a passive axis rotation are inverse transformations.

sections.heading: Recall and explain
paragraphs: Memory cue: Translate the origin; project onto new axes.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: The point stays fixed while the coordinate directions rotate. Its new coordinates are projections onto those directions. Distance from the unchanged origin is preserved.

lessons.title: Circles, systems of circles and radical axis
lessons.summary: The power of a point with respect to a circle is squared distance from its centre minus squared radius. The radical axis consists of points with equal powers for two circles.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain circles, systems of circles and radical axis.
Calculate and interpret radical-axis x, centre separation using Radical axis: 2dx=d²+r₁²−r₂².
Recognize why this claim fails: A radical axis must be a common chord of intersecting circles.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: The power of a point with respect to a circle is squared distance from its centre minus squared radius. The radical axis consists of points with equal powers for two circles.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Write each circle as x²+y²+Dx+Ey+F=0. Subtract the two equations: quadratic terms cancel and leave a line unless the circles are concentric. For centres (0,0) and (d,0), solve 2dx=d²+r₁²−r₂².
Subtract circle equations x²+y²=25 and (x−6)²+y²=9.
Quadratic terms cancel, leaving equal powers of a point.
The radical axis can exist even when the circles do not meet.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: A coaxal family combines two circle equations with a parameter while retaining a common radical axis. Three pairwise radical axes meet at a radical centre when the geometry permits, or are parallel in a limiting configuration. Actual circle intersections require additional distance-radius tests.
It exists for distinct nonconcentric circles even when they have no real intersection.

lessons.title: Cayley-Hamilton theorem
lessons.summary: The Cayley–Hamilton theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial. Substitution means matrix powers and the identity matrix, not entrywise scalar evaluation.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain cayley-hamilton theorem.
Calculate and interpret trace, determinant, largest residual entry using A²−tr(A)A+det(A)I=0.
Recognize why this claim fails: Substitute λ into each entry of A separately.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: The Cayley–Hamilton theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial. Substitution means matrix powers and the identity matrix, not entrywise scalar evaluation.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Compute p(λ)=det(λI−A). For a 2×2 matrix, p(λ)=λ²−tr(A)λ+det(A). Evaluate A²−tr(A)A+det(A)I and verify a zero matrix. If det(A)≠0, rearrange this identity to obtain A⁻¹.
Use A=[[2,1],[0,3]]. Its trace is 5 and determinant is 6.
A² has diagonal 4,9 and off-diagonal 5.
Subtraction cancels all four entries. The theorem applies to every square matrix, not only this triangular example.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: Higher powers can be reduced modulo the characteristic polynomial. The theorem does not require a matrix to be diagonalizable; Jordan blocks also satisfy it. Numerical residuals depend on floating-point precision, whereas the displayed triangular example has an exact symbolic cancellation.
Use whole matrix products and an identity matrix for the constant term.

sections.heading: Recall and explain
paragraphs: Memory cue: Characteristic polynomial, then replace λ with A.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: For A=[[2,1],[0,3]], trace=5 and determinant=6. Matrix multiplication gives A²−tr(A)A+det(A)I=0. The constant coefficient multiplies the identity matrix.

lessons.title: Laplace and Fourier transforms
lessons.summary: Transforms represent functions using different mathematical building blocks. The Laplace transform uses exponentially weighted integrals on t≥0; Fourier analysis uses oscillatory complex exponentials or trigonometric components.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain laplace and fourier transforms.
Calculate and interpret laplace transform, fourier energy / π using L{eᵃᵗ}(s)=1/(s−a); Fourier energy of A cos t+B sin t on [0,2π] is π(A²+B²).
Recognize why this claim fails: Transform tables apply without checking convergence or initial values.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: Transforms represent functions using different mathematical building blocks. The Laplace transform uses exponentially weighted integrals on t≥0; Fourier analysis uses oscillatory complex exponentials or trigonometric components.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Start from the defining integral and state its convergence region. For eᵃᵗ, the Laplace transform is 1/(s−a) for Re(s)>a. Derivatives transform with initial-value terms. Fourier coefficients follow orthogonality over a stated period and depend on the normalization convention.
Integrate e^(−(5−1)t) on t≥0; convergence requires s>a.

For the separate periodic example, orthogonality removes the cosine-sine cross term.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions

Fourier series, Fourier transforms and Laplace transforms have different domains and convergence requirements. Solve differential equations by transforming, doing algebra, then applying a justified inverse transform.

lessons.title: Complex analyticity, Cauchy formula and residues
lessons.summary: A complex function is analytic on a domain when it has a complex derivative around every point of that domain. This is stronger than having separate real-variable derivatives.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain complex analyticity, cauchy formula and residues.
Calculate and interpret residue real, residue imaginary, integral real / π, integral imaginary / π using ∮ f(z)/(z−c) dz=2πi f(c), positive simple contour.
Recognize why this claim fails: Checking Cauchy–Riemann at one point proves analyticity nearby.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: A complex function is analytic on a domain when it has a complex derivative around every point of that domain. This is stronger than having separate real-variable derivatives.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: For f=u+iv with continuous first partial derivatives, verify the Cauchy–Riemann equations uₓ=vᵧ and uᵧ=−vₓ on an open region. Cauchy integral formula then evaluates interior analytic values from a positively oriented boundary integral.
For f(z)=z² and c=2+1i, f(c)=(3)+4i.
The polynomial is analytic everywhere; the integrand has a simple pole at c with residue f(c).
Multiplication by 2πi gives the displayed real and imaginary coefficients of π. The pole must lie inside the contour.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: At an isolated pole, the residue is the coefficient of (z−c)⁻¹ in the Laurent expansion. For a simple pole of g/h with h(c)=0 and h′(c)≠0, residue=g(c)/h′(c). The residue theorem sums enclosed residues; contour orientation and singularities on the contour require separate treatment.
Analyticity needs a neighborhood and appropriate regularity, not one isolated point check.

lessons.title: Euler theorem for homogeneous functions
lessons.sourceStatus: University-authored mirrored PDF; programme verification pending
lessons.summary: A differentiable function is homogeneous of degree k if f(tx,ty)=tᵏf(x,y) on its allowed scaling domain. Euler’s theorem connects this scaling law with partial derivatives.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain euler theorem for homogeneous functions.
Calculate and interpret degree, function value, euler left side using x fₓ+y fᵧ=(a+b)f for f=xᵃyᵇ.
Recognize why this claim fails: Each individual exponent is the total homogeneity degree.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: A differentiable function is homogeneous of degree k if f(tx,ty)=tᵏf(x,y) on its allowed scaling domain. Euler’s theorem connects this scaling law with partial derivatives.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Differentiate the scaling identity with respect to t and set t=1: xfₓ+yfᵧ=kf. For f=xᵃyᵇ, the degree is a+b. Compute the derivatives independently and compare the weighted sum with degree times the original value.
Scaling both inputs by t scales f by t^(5).
x fₓ=256 and y fᵧ=384; their sum equals degree times f.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: A sum of monomials of one total degree is homogeneous; x²+y³ is not. Generalizations use additional variables and repeated differentiation. Scaling domains matter for fractional powers and functions only defined on positive inputs.
Add the exponents in each monomial and check that all terms have the same total degree.

lessons.title: Positive definite and semidefinite matrices
lessons.sourceStatus: University-authored mirrored PDF; programme verification pending
lessons.summary: A real symmetric matrix is positive definite when xᵀAx>0 for every nonzero real vector x. Positive semidefinite allows zero. These conditions describe quadratic-form curvature and covariance feasibility.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain positive definite and semidefinite matrices.
Calculate and interpret determinant, smallest eigenvalue, classification using For symmetric [[a,b],[b,d]], PD iff a>0 and ad−b²>0.
Recognize why this claim fails: Positive diagonal entries alone prove positive definiteness.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: A real symmetric matrix is positive definite when xᵀAx>0 for every nonzero real vector x. Positive semidefinite allows zero. These conditions describe quadratic-form curvature and covariance feasibility.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Use eigenvalues for a symmetric matrix: all positive gives PD, all nonnegative gives PSD. Sylvester’s criterion tests positivity of leading principal minors for PD. For a 2×2 symmetric matrix, a>0 and ad−b²>0 suffice for PD.
The matrix is real symmetric, so eigenvalues are real.
Determinant=5; smallest eigenvalue=1.38196601.
PSD needs both eigenvalues nonnegative; a zero determinant alone does not prove PSD.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: PSD requires all principal minors nonnegative, not just the leading ones. A covariance matrix is PSD; inverse-based whitening requires positive eigenvalues or a regularization/projection strategy. A nonsymmetric matrix should be assessed through its symmetric part for real quadratic forms.
Off-diagonal coupling can produce a negative eigenvalue despite positive diagonal entries.

sections.heading: Recall and explain
paragraphs: Memory cue: Symmetry first; eigenvalue signs decide curvature.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: Each cell evaluates q(x,y)=ax²+2bxy+dy². Positive values and negative values use different colors. A PSD matrix never gives a negative value; PD also excludes zero away from the origin.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: A decision tree partitions feature space using conditions chosen to improve target purity. A random forest combines many randomized trees to reduce unstable individual predictions.

sections.heading: Method and derivation

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: Random forests use bootstrap samples and feature subsampling at splits. An ensemble vote is not a probabilistic proof of correctness. Out-of-bag evaluation can estimate performance, while feature importance can be biased by feature cardinality or correlation.

lessons.title: K-means and fuzzy clustering
lessons.sourceStatus: University-authored mirrored PDF; programme verification pending
lessons.summary: K-means minimizes within-cluster squared distances by alternating nearest-centroid assignments and mean updates. Fuzzy clustering replaces hard assignments with graded memberships.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain k-means and fuzzy clustering.
Calculate and interpret centroid, within-cluster sse using K-means centroid=mean; fuzzy centroid=Σuᵢᵐxᵢ/Σuᵢᵐ.
Recognize why this claim fails: A k-means solution is guaranteed globally optimal.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: K-means minimizes within-cluster squared distances by alternating nearest-centroid assignments and mean updates. Fuzzy clustering replaces hard assignments with graded memberships.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Choose k and initialize centres, assign each point to the nearest centre, recompute each nonempty centre as a mean, and repeat until a stated convergence criterion. For fuzzy c-means, weighted centre updates use memberships raised to a fuzziness exponent m>1.
For one assigned cluster with scalar points 2,6, the centroid is their mean.
Its within-cluster squared error is the sum of squared residuals.
Fuzzy clustering uses fractional memberships; with equal memberships both points still have equal influence. Full iterative algorithms alternate assignments/memberships and centroid updates.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: K-means can settle in local minima and is sensitive to scaling, initialization and outliers. Empty clusters need an explicit recovery rule. Fuzzy membership sums to one for each point but is not automatically a calibrated probability. Compare multiple starts and assess cluster usefulness in context.
The alternating procedure generally finds a local solution; compare justified initializations.

lessons.summary: A perceptron uses a hard decision and mistake-driven updates. Neural-network backpropagation applies the chain rule to a differentiable loss across layers.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain perceptron and backpropagation.
Calculate and interpret prediction, loss, weight gradient using p=σ(wx); for label 1, dL/dw=(p−1)x.
Recognize why this claim fails: A hard threshold has the same useful derivative as sigmoid.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: A perceptron uses a hard decision and mistake-driven updates. Neural-network backpropagation applies the chain rule to a differentiable loss across layers.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: For a sigmoid neuron p=σ(wx) and binary cross-entropy with target 1, dL/dw=(p−1)x. Compute the forward prediction, loss derivative and local parameter derivative, then multiply them through the chain. Update opposite the gradient with a stated learning rate.
One logistic neuron with w=0.5,x=2 has logit 1.
Cross-entropy for target 1 is −log p=0.313261688.
The chain rule gives gradient=-0.537882843. Perceptron hard-threshold updates and differentiable backpropagation use different rules.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: The perceptron convergence result applies to linearly separable data under its assumptions. A multilayer network can represent more complex functions but needs an optimization procedure and validation. Numerical gradient checking on a small example can reveal sign or chain-rule errors.
The threshold is not differentiable at its jump and is flat elsewhere; it needs a different update rule.

lessons.summary: Evaluation asks how predictions perform on data outside training. Bias and variance describe systematic approximation error and sensitivity to the training sample, respectively.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain bias-variance and model evaluation.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: Evaluation asks how predictions perform on data outside training. Bias and variance describe systematic approximation error and sensitivity to the training sample, respectively.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Choose metrics that match the task. From TP, FP and FN, calculate precision, recall and F1. Split data to prevent leakage, tune on validation folds, and reserve a final test set. For regression, compare residual error with an appropriate baseline.
Use TP=8, FP=2, FN=3.
Precision penalizes false positives; recall penalizes false negatives.
Bias-variance concerns expected prediction error across training samples. These classification metrics do not by themselves estimate that decomposition.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: The classic squared-error decomposition separates bias², variance and irreducible noise under a defined data-generating setup. Class imbalance can make accuracy misleading. Report uncertainty and subgroup performance where meaningful; one metric cannot capture every cost of an error.
Training scores can reflect overfitting or leakage; evaluate on genuinely held-out data.

lessons.title: SIFT, HOG and image-gradient features
lessons.sourceStatus: University-authored mirrored PDF; programme verification pending
lessons.summary: Image-gradient features describe local changes in intensity. HOG aggregates orientation evidence in spatial cells; SIFT adds a keypoint and scale-space construction before forming local descriptors.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain sift, hog and image-gradient features.
Calculate and interpret magnitude, orientation degrees using Gradient magnitude=√(gₓ²+gᵧ²); orientation=atan2(gᵧ,gₓ).
Recognize why this claim fails: Gradient direction alone is a complete SIFT descriptor.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: Image-gradient features describe local changes in intensity. HOG aggregates orientation evidence in spatial cells; SIFT adds a keypoint and scale-space construction before forming local descriptors.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Compute horizontal and vertical derivatives, then magnitude √(gₓ²+gᵧ²) and orientation atan2(gᵧ,gₓ). Distribute magnitudes into orientation bins using a stated signed/unsigned convention. Normalize groups of cells to reduce contrast sensitivity.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition

lessons.sourceStatus: University-authored mirrored PDF; programme verification pending
lessons.summary: A convolutional layer shares a local kernel across an input. Most neural libraries compute cross-correlation, although they name the operation convolution. Pooling aggregates local responses.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: A convolutional layer shares a local kernel across an input. Most neural libraries compute cross-correlation, although they name the operation convolution. Pooling aggregates local responses.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: For a 1D valid kernel, multiply overlapping input and kernel values and sum at each location. True convolution reverses the kernel. Output size depends on input length, kernel size, padding, stride and dilation. Max pooling selects the largest value in each pooling window.
Input [2,5,1] and kernel [1,−1] give two valid positions.
Most deep-learning libraries call this cross-correlation convolution; true convolution flips the kernel.
Max pooling over these two outputs selects the larger response.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: Channels add another sum over input channels and separate learned kernels for outputs. Padding creates a boundary convention; stride changes sampling resolution. Pooling is not identical to learned convolution and can lose spatial detail.

lessons.summary: A recurrent model updates a hidden state over a sequence. Backpropagation through time multiplies derivatives across steps, which can make gradients shrink or grow rapidly. LSTM and GRU introduce gates controlling information flow.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain rnn, lstm, gru and gradient stability.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: A recurrent model updates a hidden state over a sequence. Backpropagation through time multiplies derivatives across steps, which can make gradients shrink or grow rapidly. LSTM and GRU introduce gates controlling information flow.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: For the linear recurrence hₜ=whₜ₋₁, h_T=wᵀh₀ and dh_T/dh₀=wᵀ. Inspect |w|<1, =1 and >1. Real recurrent networks also include inputs, activation derivatives and matrix products.
Take w=0.5, initial h₀=2, T=4.
Hidden value is 2×0.5^4.
Repeated derivative products can shrink or grow. Nonlinear RNNs also multiply activation derivatives; LSTM/GRU gates alter these paths but do not guarantee perfectly stable gradients.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: LSTM maintains a cell state with input, forget and output gates; GRU uses update and reset gates. Gates can improve gradient paths but do not guarantee stability. Gradient clipping limits large updates, while sequence length and initialization also affect training.
Gate values, recurrent weights and sequence length still determine derivative products.

lessons.summary: Attention forms a data-dependent weighted combination of values. Graph neural networks exchange messages over specified graph edges and aggregate neighbor information. Attention can supply one such aggregation rule.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain attention and graph neural networks.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: Attention forms a data-dependent weighted combination of values. Graph neural networks exchange messages over specified graph edges and aggregate neighbor information. Attention can supply one such aggregation rule.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Scaled dot-product attention calculates QKᵀ/√d, applies masks and rowwise softmax, then multiplies by V. For stable softmax subtract each row’s maximum before exponentiating. Graph layers must define neighborhood, edge use, aggregation and update functions.
Scores 2,1 are normalized after subtracting their maximum for stability.
Attention weights are 0.731058579 and 0.268941421.
Use values 0 and 10; graph neural networks can apply analogous normalized neighbor aggregation with an explicit graph and message rule.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: Weights sum to one along the chosen axis but are not automatically explanations of causal importance. Multihead attention uses several learned projections. Graph networks may oversmooth with repeated aggregation; isolated nodes and self-loops need explicit conventions. The tool illustrates two-score normalization.
Subtract the maximum first; this preserves weights and avoids overflow.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: A hidden Markov model has latent states with transition probabilities and observed emissions conditioned on states. Maximum entropy models instead normalize exponentiated feature scores for a conditional distribution.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: For one HMM path multiply the initial-state probability, all transitions and emissions. The forward algorithm sums path contributions efficiently; Viterbi chooses the highest-probability path with backpointers. Normalize each transition and emission distribution.

Multiply these conditional probabilities to score that path.
Forward inference sums across paths; Viterbi maximizes them. Maximum entropy classification normalizes exponentiated feature scores and is a different model.

lessons.title: Probabilistic grammars and dynamic-programming parsing
lessons.sourceStatus: University-authored mirrored PDF; programme verification pending
lessons.summary: A probabilistic context-free grammar assigns probabilities to production rules. A parse tree’s probability is the product of the rules applied in that tree. Dynamic programming shares repeated span computations.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain probabilistic grammars and dynamic-programming parsing.
Calculate and interpret tree probability, negative log tree probability using PCFG parse-tree probability=product of applied rule probabilities.
Recognize why this claim fails: A sentence probability always equals its best parse probability.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: A probabilistic context-free grammar assigns probabilities to production rules. A parse tree’s probability is the product of the rules applied in that tree. Dynamic programming shares repeated span computations.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: For a grammar in the required normal form, fill a chart from short spans to long spans. For each split, combine left/right subspan scores with the rule probability. Inside probability sums alternatives; a Viterbi chart maximizes and stores a backpointer.
A simple tree uses three rule applications with probabilities 0.5,0.4,0.8.
The tree probability is their product.
Inside parsing sums probabilities across valid split points and rules; Viterbi parsing takes the maximum. Rule probabilities must normalize separately for each left-hand nonterminal.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: Rule probabilities normalize per left-hand nonterminal. Ambiguous sentences can have several trees whose probabilities add to the sentence probability. Grammar transformations must preserve the intended probability semantics, and unary/epsilon rules require explicit handling.
With ambiguity, total probability includes all valid parses, not just the maximum.

sections.heading: Recall and explain
paragraphs: Memory cue: Tree rules multiply; alternative parses add.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: For S→AB, A→x and B→y, multiply the three rule probabilities: 0.5×0.4×0.8=0.16. Alternative trees would be summed for sentence probability; this diagram isolates one tree.

lessons.sourceStatus: University-authored mirrored PDF; programme verification pending
lessons.summary: Quantum pure states are unit vectors in a complex Hilbert space. Measurement probabilities follow the Born rule: squared magnitudes of projections onto the measurement outcomes.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain hilbert spaces and quantum measurement.
Calculate and interpret probability of 0, probability of 1, probability sum using P(0)=|α|²/(|α|²+|β|²) after normalization.
Recognize why this claim fails: An amplitude is already a measurement probability.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: Quantum pure states are unit vectors in a complex Hilbert space. Measurement probabilities follow the Born rule: squared magnitudes of projections onto the measurement outcomes.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Normalize amplitudes by their norm. For α|0⟩+β|1⟩ in the computational basis, P(0)=|α|² and P(1)=|β|² after normalization. Verify the probabilities add to one. An observable has eigenvalues associated with its eigenspace measurement projectors.
Real amplitudes 3,4 have squared norm 25.
Normalize by √25; measurement probabilities are squared amplitudes.
Hilbert-space amplitudes can be complex. Overall phase has no measurement effect; relative phase can affect later interference.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: Complex inner products use conjugation. Global phase is physically irrelevant, but relative phase can affect a later measurement after a basis change. Mixed states use density operators and probabilities Tr(ρΠ). The tool begins with real amplitudes to isolate normalization.
Amplitudes can be negative or complex; probability is a nonnegative squared magnitude.

objectives: Explain qubit, bloch sphere and unitary gates.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: A pure qubit can be parameterized by a polar angle θ and azimuth φ on the Bloch sphere. Unitary gates preserve inner products and state norm.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Write |ψ⟩=cos(θ/2)|0⟩+eⁱᶠsin(θ/2)|1⟩. The Bloch coordinates are (sinθ cosφ,sinθ sinφ,cosθ). Pauli-X exchanges basis amplitudes; Z changes relative sign; Hadamard mixes them. Check U†U=I before calling a matrix unitary.
Polar angle θ=60°, azimuth φ=30°.
Bloch vector=(sinθ cosφ,sinθ sinφ,cosθ).
A Pauli-X gate swaps amplitudes, so its output P(0) equals the input P(1). Unitary gates preserve the state norm.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: Bloch angles use half angles in the amplitudes. Mixed states occupy the interior of the Bloch ball. A computational-basis probability does not determine relative phase, so two different Bloch states can give the same immediate measurement statistics.
The conventional Bloch parameterization uses cos(θ/2) and sin(θ/2).

lessons.summary: Composite quantum states use tensor products of subsystem spaces. An entangled pure state cannot be written as a product of one state per subsystem. Bell states give simple maximally entangled two-qubit examples.
prerequisites: Calculus, probability or linear algebra as used below
objectives: Explain tensor products, bell states and entanglement.
Calculate and interpret p(00), p(11), joint probability sum, reduced-state purity using |ψ⟩=cosθ|00⟩+sinθ|11⟩.
Recognize why this claim fails: Any correlated pair of measurement outcomes proves entanglement.

sections.heading: Concept and intuition
paragraphs: Composite quantum states use tensor products of subsystem spaces. An entangled pure state cannot be written as a product of one state per subsystem. Bell states give simple maximally entangled two-qubit examples.

sections.heading: Method and derivation
paragraphs: Fix the basis order |00⟩,|01⟩,|10⟩,|11⟩. A product state expands by multiplying subsystem amplitudes. For cosθ|00⟩+sinθ|11⟩, both nonzero terms imply Schmidt rank two; at θ=45° their equal magnitudes give a Bell state.
The tensor-product basis order is |00⟩,|01⟩,|10⟩,|11⟩.
P(00)=0.5, P(11)=0.5; the other two probabilities are zero.
At θ=45° this is a Bell state. For nonzero amplitudes on both basis states the pure state is entangled; measurement correlations alone are not a universal entanglement test.

sections.heading: Connections and conditions
paragraphs: Taking a partial trace produces each subsystem’s density matrix. Its purity below one signals entanglement for a globally pure bipartite state. Classical correlations in mixed states are not alone sufficient to prove entanglement. Measurement on one part yields correlated outcomes without enabling faster-than-light signalling.
Mixed classical states can also be correlated; use the appropriate state-level criterion.

sections.heading: Recall and explain
paragraphs: Memory cue: Tensor product combines systems; factorability tests pure-state entanglement.

sections.heading: Read the visualization
paragraphs: Only |00⟩ and |11⟩ have nonzero amplitudes. Squaring cos(45°) and sin(45°) gives their measurement probabilities. At 45° they are equal; at 0° or 90° the state is a product state.
For the initial values, P(00) = 0.5; P(11) = 0.5; Joint probability sum = 1; Reduced-state purity = 0.5. |ψ⟩=cosθ|00⟩+sinθ|11⟩
